header_line: Real PYQ Bank - Physics (Class XII level only, organized by chapter)
instructions: Every Class-XII-level Physics question from the real past papers you provided, organized by chapter. Degree-level content has been excluded since it's beyond this exam's actual syllabus depth. Options are unticked - a simple, clear Answer and solution is directly below each question.

questions.q: Which physical quantity has dimension MLT^-2*A^-2?
questions.given: A physical quantity with dimensional formula M*L*T^-2*A^-2.
questions.concept: Ampere's force law per unit length between two parallel current-carrying wires: F/L = mu0*I1*I2/(2*pi*d), so mu0 = F*d/(I1*I2*L).
calculation: Idea: the dimension M*L*T^-2*A^-2 looks like force divided by current squared. Ampere's force law gives that.
Force per unit length between two parallel wires: F/L = mu0*I1*I2/(2*pi*d). So mu0 = F*d/(I1*I2*L). The number 2*pi has no dimension.
Dimension of force F = M*L*T^-2. Dimension of d = L. Dimension of L (wire length) = L. Dimension of I1*I2 = A*A = A^2.
Substitute: [mu0] = (M*L*T^-2 * L)/(A^2 * L).
Cancel one L from top and bottom: [mu0] = M*L*T^-2*A^-2.
Check other options: magnetic field B = F/(I*L) gives M*T^-2*A^-1. Magnetic moment = I*area gives A*L^2. Torsion constant = torque/angle gives M*L^2*T^-2. None match.
So the quantity is the permeability of free space, mu0.
questions.info: Permeability of free space mu0 = 4*pi*10^-7 T*m/A was an exact fixed value before the 2019 SI redefinition; it's now an experimentally measured (though extremely precise) constant.
questions.trick: Whenever a dimension question shows A^-2, think 'two currents are involved' - that's a strong signal for mu0, since most other magnetic quantities (field, moment) involve only A^1 or A^-1.

questions.q: What is the dimension of 'thermal conductivity'?
questions.given: Find the dimensional formula of thermal conductivity k.
questions.concept: Fourier's law of heat conduction: Q/t = k*A*(delta T)/x, so k = (Q/t)*x/(A*delta T).
calculation: Fourier's law: Q/t = k*A*(delta T)/x. Here Q/t is heat flow per second, A is area, delta T is temperature difference, x is thickness.
Rearrange for k: k = (Q/t)*x/(A*delta T).
Q/t is energy per time = power. Energy = M*L^2*T^-2, so power = M*L^2*T^-3.
Thickness x = L. Area A = L^2. Temperature difference delta T = K.
Substitute: [k] = (M*L^2*T^-3 * L)/(L^2 * K).
Top = M*L^3*T^-3. Bottom = L^2*K. Divide: L^3/L^2 = L.
[k] = M*L*T^-3*K^-1. This matches option C.
questions.info: Thermal conductivity's dimension is easy to confuse with specific heat (M*L^2*T^-2*K^-1), which is a deliberate distractor option here - the key difference is the extra length in thermal conductivity's formula.
questions.trick: Derive from the familiar formula (rate of heat flow = k*A*delta T/x) instead of memorising k's dimension directly - cancelling area and length on the fly avoids confusing it with specific/latent heat.

questions.q: Which pair are dimensionless quantities? (i) Refractive index, (ii) Moment of inertia, (iii) Strain, (iv) Surface tension
questions.given: Four quantities: (i) refractive index, (ii) moment of inertia, (iii) strain, (iv) surface tension.
questions.concept: A quantity is dimensionless when it is a ratio of two quantities of the same type (same dimensions cancel out).
calculation: Rule: a quantity is dimensionless if it is a ratio of two quantities of the same kind. The units cancel.
(i) Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum / speed in medium = c/v. Speed over speed, so dimensionless.
(iii) Strain = change in length / original length. Length over length, so dimensionless.
(ii) Moment of inertia I = m*r^2 has dimension M*L^2. Not dimensionless.
(iv) Surface tension = force/length = (M*L*T^-2)/L = M*T^-2. Not dimensionless.
Dimensionless ones are (i) and (iii).
This matches the option (i) and (iii).
questions.info: Other common dimensionless NCERT quantities worth remembering: plane angle (radian), relative density, Reynolds number, and Poisson's ratio.
questions.trick: Scan each quantity's definition for 'ratio of two same-type quantities' - that pattern instantly flags dimensionless quantities without working out full dimensional formulas.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an SI unit?
questions.given: Options: kilogram, ampere, litre, kelvin.
questions.concept: SI units are a fixed defined set (base units metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela, plus their derived combinations); some everyday metric units are accepted for use with SI but are not themselves SI units.
calculation: SI base units are: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela. Other SI units are made from these.
Kilogram is the SI base unit of mass. So it is an SI unit.
Ampere is the SI base unit of electric current. So it is an SI unit.
Kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature. So it is an SI unit.
Litre is a unit of volume: 1 litre = 10^-3 m^3. The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre (m^3). Litre is only accepted for use with SI, it is not an SI unit.
So the one that is NOT an SI unit is litre.
questions.info: Other common non-SI-but-accepted units include minute, hour, degree, and tonne - all fine to use alongside SI but not formally SI units themselves.
questions.trick: When a list mixes obvious base SI units with one everyday/common unit (litre, calorie, bar), that everyday unit is almost always the non-SI answer.

questions.q: Which of the following quantities has dimension formula of M^1 L^0 T^-2?
questions.given: Target dimension: M^1 L^0 T^-2.
questions.concept: Surface tension = force per unit length, so dimension = [MLT^-2]/[L].
calculation: Write each option's dimension and compare with M^1 L^0 T^-2.
Angular frequency = 1/time, dimension T^-1 (option A, no mass).
Momentum = mass * velocity = M L T^-1 (option B).
Kinetic energy = M L^2 T^-2 (option C).
Surface tension = force / length = (M L T^-2)/(L) = M L^0 T^-2.
This equals M^1 L^0 T^-2. Matches option D.
questions.info: Surface tension has the same dimension as spring constant (force per length), M T^-2, and its SI unit N/m equals J/m^2.
questions.trick: Dimension with no L and only M, T^-2 in the list: think N/m, which is surface tension or spring constant.

questions.q: The current I through resistance R on applying voltage V was measured as below. V = (100 +- 4) V and I = (10 +- 0.3) A. Find the percentage error in R.
questions.given: V = 100 V with error 4 V, I = 10 A with error 0.3 A; R = V/I.
questions.concept: For a quotient, maximum percentage errors add.
calculation: Formula: R = V/I, so percentage error in R = percentage error in V + percentage error in I.
Percentage error in V = (4/100)*100 = 4 percent.
Percentage error in I = (0.3/10)*100 = 3 percent.
Percentage error in R = 4 + 3.
= 7 percent.
This matches option B.
questions.info: For products and quotients errors add; for sums and differences absolute errors add. For a power x^n, percentage error is multiplied by n.
questions.trick: In division or multiplication never subtract errors: just add the percentage errors (4 + 3 = 7).

questions.q: If the time period of oscillation of a pendulum is measured as 1.5 seconds using a stop watch with least count of 1/2 second, the permissible error in the measurement is:
questions.given: Measured T = 1.5 s, least count = 0.5 s.
questions.concept: The permissible (maximum) error equals the least count; percentage error = (least count / measured value)*100.
calculation: Formula: permissible error = least count of the instrument.
Percentage error = (least count / measured value) * 100.
Substitute: (0.5/1.5) * 100.
This matches option C.
questions.info: Least count is the smallest reading an instrument can measure; a smaller least count means higher precision. Measuring many oscillations reduces the percentage error.
questions.trick: Percentage error = LC/value * 100: 0.5 out of 1.5 is one third, i.e. 33.3 percent.

questions.q: Object at origin, initial velocity v0=i+j, acted on by some force. Which position equation applies?
questions.given: Particle starts at origin, initial velocity v_0 = i+j (v_x0=1, v_y0=1 m/s), moving under a constant force (constant acceleration).
questions.concept: For constant acceleration motion, r(t) must satisfy r(0)=0 and dr/dt at t=0 = v_0; differentiating the candidate position equation twice also gives the constant acceleration vector, which must match the force/mass given in the problem.
calculation: Given: v_0 = i + j, so v_x0 = 1 and v_y0 = 1 m/s. Position at t=0 is the origin.
Test: for each option, differentiate r to get v and put t=0. It must give i + j.
Option A (read as i(2.5t^2+t)+j(t-t^2)): v = i(5t + 1) + j(1 - 2t), so v(0) = i + j. It matches v_0, so check acceleration later.
Option B: v = i(5t - 1) + j(1 + 3t), so v(0) = -i + j. This does not match.
Option C: v = 1.5i + 2t j, so v(0) = 1.5i. This does not match.
Option D: r = i(2.5t^2 + t) + j(t - 1.5t^2). v = i(5t + 1) + j(1 - 3t). At t=0, v = i + j. This matches.
Second derivative gives acceleration: option A gives a = 5i - 2j, option D gives a = 5i - 3j. The force in the full problem gives a = 5i - 3j, so A is ruled out.
So the correct position equation is r = i(2.5t^2 + t) + j(t - 1.5t^2).
questions.info: Whenever acceleration is constant, position is always quadratic in t: r(t)=r_0+v_0*t+0.5*a*t^2 -- so you can read off v_0 and a directly from the coefficients of t and t^2 instead of memorising a separate formula for each axis.
questions.trick: Just differentiate each option once and plug t=0 -- this instantly kills options whose initial velocity doesn't match v_0, often leaving only one choice (here you additionally need the acceleration coefficient to pick between two survivors).

questions.q: A 15kg particle, constant acceleration 3 m/s^2 from rest. Find momentum and velocity at t=0.5, 1.5, 2, 3 sec.
questions.given: Mass m=15kg, constant acceleration a=3 m/s^2, starts from rest (u=0); need p and v at t=0.5, 1.5, 2, 3 s.
questions.concept: Kinematics from rest: v=u+at=at (since u=0); momentum p=mv.
calculation: Given: m = 15 kg, a = 3 m/s^2, starts from rest so u = 0.
Formulas: v = u + a*t = a*t (since u = 0). Momentum p = m*v.
Result: p = 22.5 (v = 1.5), 67.5 (v = 4.5), 90 (v = 6), 135 (v = 9). This matches option D.
questions.info: Since acceleration is constant, momentum vs time is also a straight line through the origin (p=m*a*t), so you could equally well scale the t=0.5s answer by 3, 4 and 6 to get the rest.
questions.trick: Compute v at the smallest time first, then just scale it up proportionally for the other times instead of recomputing v=at each time from scratch.

questions.q: A ball projected at t=0. At height 15m, velocity (m/s) v=8.0i+10j. Find the maximum height reached. (g=10 m/s^2)
questions.given: At height h=15m, velocity v=8.0i+10j m/s (v_y=10 m/s here), g=10 m/s^2, projectile motion.
questions.concept: Vertical motion only: v_y^2 = v_y0^2 - 2*g*h (v_y0 is vertical launch speed), and max height H = v_y0^2/(2g).
calculation: Given: at h = 15 m, v_y = 10 m/s (the j-part). g = 10 m/s^2. The i-part 8.0 is horizontal and does not change, so ignore it.
Formula (vertical motion): v_y^2 = v_y0^2 - 2*g*h.
Rearrange: v_y0^2 = v_y^2 + 2*g*h.
So v_y0 = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s (launch speed upward).
Max height: at the top v_y = 0, so H = v_y0^2/(2*g).
H = 400/(2*10) = 400/20 = 20 m. This matches option A.
questions.info: The horizontal component (8.0 m/s) is irrelevant for max height since horizontal and vertical motions are independent in projectile motion -- it's only given here to test if you get distracted by it.
questions.trick: Ignore the i-component entirely for a 'max height' question -- only the j-component (vertical velocity) ever matters, so you can solve this in two lines.

questions.q: A ball thrown upward (g=9.8 m/s^2). What is its acceleration during upward motion and at the highest point respectively?
questions.given: Ball thrown vertically upward, g=9.8 m/s^2 (downward, constant throughout the motion).
questions.concept: Acceleration due to gravity is constant in magnitude and direction (always downward, -g) throughout free flight, regardless of the instantaneous velocity.
calculation: Key idea: only gravity acts on a thrown ball (ignore air). Gravity gives a constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s^2.
Take upward as positive. Then acceleration = -9.8 m/s^2 always.
While going up: velocity is upward, but acceleration is still downward. a = -9.8 m/s^2.
At the highest point: velocity is momentarily 0, but gravity still pulls. a = -9.8 m/s^2.
Option check: -9.8 and 0 is wrong, since a is not zero at the top. -9.8 and +9.8 is wrong, since a does not change sign. +9.8 and 0 is wrong on both.
Correct: -9.8 m/s^2 and -9.8 m/s^2.
questions.info: A very common exam trap is to say acceleration is zero at the highest point because velocity is zero there -- velocity being zero does NOT mean acceleration is zero; here it's precisely because acceleration stays -9.8 m/s^2 at the top that velocity keeps changing sign (motion reverses) right after.
questions.trick: Whenever you see 'acceleration at the highest point of projectile/vertical throw' as a question, the answer is almost always '-g (unchanged)' -- it's a standard trap question testing velocity vs acceleration confusion.

questions.q: A position-time graph is a straight line at 30 degrees to the x-axis. The ball is moving with:
questions.given: Position-time (x-t) graph is a straight line inclined at 30 degrees to the x(time)-axis.
questions.concept: Velocity = slope of the x-t graph (v=dx/dt); a straight line means constant slope, hence constant velocity.
calculation: Key idea: in a position-time (x-t) graph, velocity = slope = dx/dt.
The graph is a straight line at 30 degrees to the x-axis (here the x-axis is the time axis).
Slope = tan(30 degrees) = 1/sqrt(3) = 0.577. This is a fixed number.
A straight line has the same slope everywhere. So v = dx/dt does not change with time.
Constant velocity means acceleration a = dv/dt = 0.
Option check: increasing velocity or increasing/decreasing acceleration would need a curved x-t graph. They are wrong.
Correct: the ball moves with constant velocity.
questions.info: If the x-t graph were curved instead of straight, the slope (velocity) would keep changing, which is what a non-zero, non-constant acceleration looks like on a position-time graph.
questions.trick: On an x-t graph: straight line = constant velocity (zero acceleration); curved line = changing velocity (acceleration present) -- no calculation needed, just recognise the shape.

questions.q: A trolley (20kg) and hanging block (3kg) connected by a string, 30N applied force, kinetic friction coefficient 0.06. Find acceleration and tension. (g=10 m/s^2)
questions.given: Trolley m1=20kg on a rough horizontal table, hanging block m2=3kg connected by a string over a pulley, kinetic friction coefficient mu=0.06 between trolley and table, g=10 m/s^2.
questions.concept: Connected-system Newton's second law: the hanging block's weight drives the system against friction on the trolley; treat trolley+block as one system to find a, then use the block's equation to find T.
calculation: Setup: trolley m1 = 20 kg on a rough table, hanging block m2 = 3 kg on a string over a pulley, mu = 0.06, g = 10 m/s^2.
Friction on trolley: f = mu*m1*g = 0.06*20*10 = 12 N.
Pull from the hanging block weight: m2*g = 3*10 = 30 N (this is the 30 N force in the question).
Treat trolley and block as one system: (m1 + m2)*a = m2*g - f.
Tension from the block alone: m2*g - T = m2*a, so T = m2*(g - a).
Nearest option is a = 0.79 m/s^2, T = 27.63 N (small rounding difference). Others differ a lot.
questions.info: This is the standard 'connected bodies with friction' setup -- always start with the system equation (ignore internal tension) to get a first, then isolate one body to solve for T, rather than writing two simultaneous equations from scratch.
questions.trick: Compute friction and driving force separately first (12N and 30N here), then it's just one subtraction and one division to get acceleration -- no need to set up full free-body equations for both masses.

questions.q: A 5kg object slides at constant 12 m/s on a frictionless table. The force needed to keep it moving at that velocity is:
questions.given: Object mass 5kg, moving at constant velocity 12 m/s on a frictionless table.
questions.concept: Newton's first law: an object moving at constant velocity has zero net force acting on it (no acceleration needed to maintain constant velocity).
calculation: Given: m = 5 kg, constant velocity 12 m/s, frictionless table.
Constant velocity means velocity does not change, so acceleration a = 0.
Newton's second law: F_net = m*a = 5*0 = 0 N.
On a frictionless table nothing opposes the motion, so no force is needed to keep it moving (Newton's first law).
Option check: 15 N, 4 N and 1 N would cause acceleration. They are wrong.
Force needed = 0 N.
questions.info: This directly tests the common misconception (from everyday experience with friction) that a constant push is needed to keep something moving -- that's only true when friction/resistance needs to be countered.
questions.trick: Spot the word 'frictionless' plus 'constant velocity' together -- that combo almost always means the answer is 0 N, no calculation needed.

questions.q: Blocks A(5.0kg), B(3.0kg), C(2.0kg) on a frictionless surface, connected by strings. C is pulled with 50N. Find the ratio T2/T1 (B-C string to A-B string tension).
questions.given: Blocks A=5kg, B=3kg, C=2kg in a line on a frictionless surface (A-B-C order), connected by strings, C is pulled with F=50N.
questions.concept: Common acceleration a=F_total/m_total for the whole chain; tension in each string only needs to accelerate the mass behind it (away from the pull).
calculation: Setup: A = 5 kg, B = 3 kg, C = 2 kg in a line on a smooth surface. C is pulled with F = 50 N. T1 joins A-B and T2 joins B-C.
Total mass = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 kg.
Common acceleration: a = F/(total mass) = 50/10 = 5 m/s^2.
T1 is the only pull on A: T1 = m_A*a = 5*5 = 25 N.
T2 pulls A and B together: T2 = (m_A + m_B)*a = (5 + 3)*5 = 8*5 = 40 N.
Check with C: F - T2 = m_C*a gives 50 - 40 = 10 = 2*5. Correct.
questions.info: In a pulled chain of blocks, tension always increases as you move toward the end being pulled, since each successive string has to accelerate more mass behind it.
questions.trick: You never need to solve simultaneous equations for chain-of-blocks problems -- just find common acceleration once, then multiply by the cumulative mass behind each string.

questions.q: A ball projected at angle theta_0 with speed u. Find the horizontal Range.
questions.given: Projectile launched with speed u at angle theta_0 to the horizontal; need the horizontal range formula.
questions.concept: Projectile range formula: R = (u^2/g)*sin(2*theta_0), derived from R = (horizontal velocity)*(time of flight).
calculation: Given: launch speed u at angle theta_0. Horizontal speed = u*cos(theta_0). Vertical speed = u*sin(theta_0).
Time of flight: ball returns to the same level, so 0 = u*sin(theta_0)*T - (1/2)*g*T^2.
Take T common: T*(u*sin(theta_0) - (1/2)*g*T) = 0. T = 0 is the start, so u*sin(theta_0) = (1/2)*g*T, which gives T = 2*u*sin(theta_0)/g.
Range = horizontal speed * time = u*cos(theta_0) * 2*u*sin(theta_0)/g.
R = 2*u^2*sin(theta_0)*cos(theta_0)/g.
Use 2*sin(theta)*cos(theta) = sin(2*theta). So R = (u^2/g)*sin(2*theta_0).
This matches option D.
questions.info: Range is maximum at theta_0=45 degrees (since sin(2*theta_0) maxes out at 1), and the same range is obtained for complementary angles like 30 and 60 degrees -- a frequently tested fact.
questions.trick: Just memorise R=(u^2/g)*sin(2*theta_0) directly -- it's one of the most repeated NCERT formulas, so recognise it on sight rather than re-deriving it.

questions.q: Rahul (60kg) stands on frictionless ice, kicks a 2.0kg box giving it velocity (3.0 m/s)i. What is Rahul's velocity after the kick?
questions.given: Rahul mass=60kg, box mass=2.0kg, system initially at rest on frictionless ice; box gets velocity +3.0i m/s after the kick.
questions.concept: Conservation of linear momentum: total momentum before = total momentum after (no external horizontal force on the Rahul+box system).
calculation: Key idea: no outside horizontal force on Rahul + box (frictionless ice), so total momentum stays the same.
Formula: m1*v1 + m2*v2 (after) = 0 (before, both at rest).
Put numbers: 60*V + 2.0*3.0 = 0.
Minus sign means Rahul moves opposite to the box. V = -(0.1 m/s)i.
questions.info: This is the same physics as recoil of a gun -- the much heavier body (Rahul) recoils with a much smaller speed than the lighter body (box) because momentum, not speed, is what balances out.
questions.trick: Just use m1*v1 = -m2*v2 directly (momentum conservation from rest) -- the negative sign tells you the direction is opposite to the kicked object, no need for full vector algebra.

questions.q: Meena drives a car (mass m) on a circular path (radius R), static friction coefficient mu. Find the max speed without slipping.
questions.given: Car mass m, circular path radius R, coefficient of static friction mu between tyres and road (flat/unbanked road).
questions.concept: Centripetal force needed for circular motion is supplied entirely by friction on an unbanked road: friction force = mu*m*g = m*v^2/R.
calculation: Key idea: on a flat road, friction gives the centripetal force. At the maximum speed friction is at its limit.
Maximum static friction = mu*N = mu*m*g (since N = m*g on a flat road).
Centripetal force needed = m*v^2/R.
Equate: m*v^2/R = mu*m*g.
Cancel m from both sides: v^2/R = mu*g.
Multiply by R: v^2 = mu*g*R.
Take the square root: v_max = sqrt(mu*R*g). This matches option D.
questions.info: Notice the mass of the car cancels out entirely -- the maximum safe speed on a flat curve doesn't depend on how heavy the car is, only on mu, g and R.
questions.trick: Recognise this as the standard 'unbanked curve' formula v=sqrt(mu*g*R) -- if the road were banked instead, the formula would change to include the banking angle, so check the question doesn't mention banking before applying this.

questions.q: A 20kg block on a rough surface. A 50N horizontal force is applied but the block does NOT move. What is the friction force? (g=10 m/s^2)
questions.given: Block mass=20kg on a rough surface, applied horizontal force=50N, block remains stationary (does not move), g=10 m/s^2.
questions.concept: Static friction is a self-adjusting (variable) force that exactly balances the applied force up to its maximum limit, as long as the object stays in equilibrium (a=0).
calculation: Given: m = 20 kg, applied force = 50 N, block does not move.
Not moving means acceleration a = 0, so net horizontal force = 0.
Forces along the surface: applied force 50 N one way, friction f the other way.
Balance: f = 50 N.
Why not mu*m*g? Static friction adjusts itself to match the push, up to a limit. It is not always at its limit value.
Option check: 1000 N and 200 N are too large, 0 N would let the block move. Only 50 N balances.
Friction force = 50 N.
questions.info: Static friction is NOT automatically equal to mu_s*N -- that product only gives the maximum possible static friction; the actual friction is whatever is needed for equilibrium, up to that maximum (here it's simply 50N since the block stays still).
questions.trick: Whenever the object 'does not move' under an applied force, skip any mu or normal-force calculation entirely -- friction just equals the applied force, full stop.

questions.q: Mohan (60kg) runs up a 5m staircase rise in 6s. Find his average power. (g=10 m/s^2)
questions.given: Mohan mass=60kg, vertical rise h=5m, time t=6s, g=10 m/s^2.
questions.concept: Average power = work done against gravity / time taken; work done = m*g*h (gain in gravitational potential energy).
calculation: Given: m = 60 kg, rise h = 5 m, time t = 6 s, g = 10 m/s^2.
Formula: Power = Work/time, and Work done against gravity = m*g*h.
This matches the option 0.5 kW.
questions.info: This calculation only accounts for the vertical rise (potential energy gained), ignoring any horizontal distance walked or kinetic energy changes, since those are usually considered negligible or not asked for in this type of question.
questions.trick: For 'power to climb stairs/a height' questions, always use P=mgh/t directly -- don't overthink it with forces or friction unless the question explicitly mentions them.

questions.q: A point mass has velocity v=(1.0)i+(3.0)j m/s, experiencing force F=-(2.0)i+(4.0)j+(5.0)k N. Find the power delivered by the force at that instant.
questions.given: Velocity v=(1.0)i+(3.0)j m/s, Force F=-(2.0)i+(4.0)j+(5.0)k N.
questions.concept: Instantaneous power delivered by a force = dot product of force and velocity: P = F.v.
calculation: Formula: power from a force = dot product, P = F . v = Fx*vx + Fy*vy + Fz*vz.
Components: F = (-2.0, 4.0, 5.0) N and v = (1.0, 3.0, 0) m/s. There is no k-term in v, so vz = 0.
Positive power means the force adds energy to the mass. This matches 10 W.
questions.info: Power can be negative if the force opposes the velocity direction in that component (like the x-component here contributing -2W) -- the final positive 10W just means the force overall does positive work at this instant.
questions.trick: Since velocity has no k-component, you can ignore the k-component of force entirely (5.0k contributes zero to the dot product) -- saves you a multiplication step.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a thin circular ring with radius R with axis along diameter is given by:
questions.given: Thin ring of mass M and radius R, axis along a diameter.
questions.concept: Perpendicular axis theorem for a planar ring: I_z = I_x + I_y, with I_x = I_y by symmetry.
calculation: Formula: perpendicular axis theorem, I_z = I_x + I_y for a planar body.
For a ring, the axis through the centre perpendicular to its plane has I_z = MR^2.
By symmetry, two perpendicular diameters give equal moments: I_x = I_y = I.
So 2*I = MR^2.
This matches option B.
questions.info: For a ring: I about centre axis = MR^2, about diameter = (1/2)MR^2, about tangent in its plane = (3/2)MR^2, about tangent perpendicular = 2MR^2.
questions.trick: Option with M^2 or missing R^2 is dimensionally wrong; ring about diameter is always half of MR^2.

questions.q: A bullet of mass 0.03 kg moving with a speed of 90 m s^-1 enters a heavy wooden block and is stopped after a distance of 60 cm. What is the average resistive force exerted by the block on the bullet?
questions.given: m = 0.03 kg, u = 90 m/s, final v = 0, d = 60 cm = 0.6 m.
questions.concept: Work-energy theorem: work done by resistive force equals loss in kinetic energy.
calculation: Formula (work-energy theorem): F*d = initial KE - final KE = (1/2)*m*u^2 - 0.
Distance d = 60 cm = 0.6 m.
This matches option B.
questions.info: Doubling the speed of a bullet quadruples the penetration depth in the same block, since KE grows as v^2 while the resistive force stays constant.

questions.q: The decrease in potential energy of a ball of mass 10 kg that falls from height of 50 cm is (take g = 10 m/s^2):
questions.concept: Change in gravitational potential energy = m*g*h for a fall through height h.
calculation: Formula: decrease in PE = m*g*h.
Convert height: 50 cm = 0.5 m.
Decrease in PE = 100 * 0.5.
This matches option A.
questions.info: Decrease in PE equals gain in KE (if no air resistance), so the ball hits the ground with KE = 50 J.
questions.trick: Always convert cm to m first: the common trap here is using 50 instead of 0.5, which gives 5000 J.

questions.q: A man goes 6 m north. Then he goes 8 m towards east. What is his displacement?
questions.given: 6 m north, then 8 m east (perpendicular directions).
questions.concept: Displacement is the straight line from start to end; use Pythagoras for perpendicular legs.
calculation: Formula: displacement = straight-line distance from start to end point.
North and east are perpendicular, so the two legs form a right triangle.
This matches option B (distance travelled is 14 m, but displacement is 10 m).
questions.info: Distance (14 m) is a scalar path length; displacement (10 m) is a vector, and displacement is never greater than distance.
questions.trick: Spot Pythagorean triples: 6-8-10 and 3-4-5 save all the calculation.

questions.q: A force of 6 N acts on a particle along the direction, making angle of 60 degrees with vertical. Its vertical component will be:
questions.given: F = 6 N, angle with the vertical = 60 degrees.
questions.concept: Component along a line = F*cos(angle with that line).
calculation: Formula: component along a direction = F * cos(angle between force and that direction).
The angle is measured from the vertical, so vertical component = F*cos(60 degrees).
cos(60 degrees) = 1/2.
F_vertical = 6 * (1/2).
This matches option D.
questions.info: If the angle were given from the horizontal, the vertical component would use sine instead: F*sin(theta). Always check which axis the angle is measured from.
questions.trick: Angle with an axis means cos for that axis, sin for the other one.

questions.q: A 200 m long train is moving with a uniform velocity of 45 km/h. Calculate the time taken by the train to cross the bridge of length 800 m.
questions.given: Train length = 200 m, bridge length = 800 m, speed = 45 km/h.
questions.concept: To cross a bridge, the train covers bridge length plus its own length at constant speed.
calculation: Formula: time = total distance / speed.
Total distance to cross = 200 + 800 = 1000 m.
Convert speed: 45 km/h = 45 * (5/18) m/s = 12.5 m/s.
This matches option A.
questions.info: Crossing a pole needs only the train length; crossing a bridge or platform needs train length plus bridge length.
questions.trick: To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18: 45 km/h = 12.5 m/s.

questions.q: A plane in level flight has two wings (20 m^2 each). Air speed is 198 km/h over the lower wing and 270 km/h over the upper wing. What is the plane's mass? (air density=1 kg/m^3)
questions.given: Wing area 20 m^2 each (2 wings), air density=1 kg/m^3, lower surface speed=198 km/h, upper surface speed=270 km/h.
questions.concept: Bernoulli's principle: P + 1/2 rho v^2 = const (same height), so pressure difference deltaP = P_lower - P_upper = 1/2 rho (v_upper^2 - v_lower^2); lift force = deltaP * total wing area = weight = mg.
calculation: Idea: Bernoulli's principle: P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 stays constant. Faster air above means lower pressure above, so the plane gets lift.
Pressure difference: delta P = (1/2)*rho*(v_upper^2 - v_lower^2).
Squares: 75^2 = 5625 and 55^2 = 3025. Difference = 2600.
Total wing area = 2*20 = 40 m^2. Lift = delta P*A = 1300*40 = 52000 N.
Level flight: lift = weight, so m*g = 52000.
m = 52000/9.8 = 5306.1 kg. This matches option A.
questions.info: This is the standard explanation for aircraft lift: faster airflow over the curved upper wing surface creates lower pressure there (Bernoulli), and the pressure difference across both wings must equal the plane's weight for level flight.
questions.trick: Always convert km/h to m/s first (divide by 3.6) before plugging into Bernoulli's v^2 term, since a unit slip here is the most common error in these problems.

questions.q: A block (0.2 m^2 area) sits on a frictionless surface with a 0.20mm liquid layer. A 0.010 kgf force moves it at 0.075 m/s. Find the coefficient of viscosity.
questions.given: Area A=0.2 m^2, liquid layer thickness d=0.20 mm=2x10^-4 m, force F=0.010 kgf, velocity v=0.075 m/s.
questions.concept: Newton's law of viscosity for a thin layer: F = eta * A * v / d, so eta = F*d/(A*v).
calculation: Formula (Newton's law of viscosity): F = eta*A*v/d. So eta = F*d/(A*v).
Convert force: take 1 kgf = 10 N (usual exam value; 9.8 N is more accurate). F = 0.010*10 = 0.1 N.
Convert thickness: d = 0.20 mm = 0.20*10^-3 m = 2*10^-4 m.
With g = 9.8 you get 1.31*10^-3, which is still closest to this option. Answer: 1.33*10^-3 Pa.s.
questions.info: Coefficient of viscosity has units Pa.s (or poise in CGS, 1 Pa.s = 10 poise); this thin-layer formula F=eta*A*v/d is just the viscous-drag analog of a block sliding on a lubricated surface.
questions.trick: In 'thin liquid film' problems, picture it as a simple uniform velocity gradient v/d (not a parabolic profile) - this lets you jump straight to eta=F*d/(A*v) without setting up calculus.

questions.q: A hydraulic lift raises a 2000kg car; piston area 375 cm^2. The bigger piston is 2m higher than the smaller. Oil density 800 kg/m^3. What pressure must the smaller piston bear?
questions.given: Car mass=2000 kg, piston area=375 cm^2=0.0375 m^2, height difference between pistons=2 m, oil density=800 kg/m^3.
questions.concept: Pascal's law for a hydraulic lift with pistons at different heights: pressure needed at the lower (smaller) piston = pressure needed to support the load at the upper piston + hydrostatic pressure of the oil column of height h: P_small = Mg/A + rho*g*h.
calculation: Idea: Pascal's law. Pressure at the small piston must hold the car's pressure at the big piston plus the oil column of height h.
Formula: P_small = M*g/A + rho*g*h.
Nearest option is 5.37*10^5 N/m^2 (small rounding difference). Others are far off.
questions.info: In hydraulic lifts the height difference between pistons genuinely matters, because pressure in a connected fluid changes with depth (P = P0 + rho*g*h), unlike idealized textbook diagrams that show both pistons at the same level.
questions.trick: Spot whether the problem mentions a height difference between pistons - if it does, add/subtract rho*g*h to the plain Pascal's-law answer; if not, the heights cancel and you only need Mg/A.

questions.q: At what depth in water does pressure equal 3x atmospheric pressure? (atm=10 N/cm^2, g=9.8 m/s^2)
questions.given: Atmospheric pressure=10 N/cm^2=1x10^5 N/m^2, target total pressure=3x atmospheric, g=9.8 m/s^2, water density=1000 kg/m^3.
questions.concept: Pressure at depth h in a fluid: P = P_atm + rho*g*h.
calculation: Formula: P = P_atm + rho*g*h. Here P_atm = 10 N/cm^2. Convert: 1 cm^2 = 10^-4 m^2, so 10 N/cm^2 = 10 / 10^-4 = 10^5 N/m^2.
Total pressure wanted = 3 x P_atm = 3 x 10^5 N/m^2.
Substitute: 3 x 10^5 = 1 x 10^5 + 1000 x 9.8 x h.
Subtract 1 x 10^5 from both sides: 2 x 10^5 = 9800 x h.
Divide both sides by 9800: h = 200000 / 9800.
h = 20.41 m, which is about 20.4 m.
Check: only the extra 2 x P_atm comes from water, so depth = 2 x (10 m of water per atm) = about 20 m. Matches 20.4 m.
questions.info: Atmospheric pressure (~10^5 Pa) is roughly equal to the pressure from a 10.3 m column of water, so every extra ~10 m of depth adds roughly one more atmosphere of pressure - a handy quick estimate.
questions.trick: Remember water pressure rises by about 1 atm per 10 m of depth - '3x atm needs 2 extra atm' instantly gives a sanity-check estimate of ~20 m before doing exact arithmetic.

questions.q: If longitudinal strain for a wire is 0.02 and its Poisson's ratio is 0.5, find lateral strain.
questions.given: Longitudinal strain = 0.02, Poisson's ratio sigma = 0.5.
questions.concept: Poisson's ratio = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (magnitudes).
calculation: Formula: Poisson's ratio sigma = (lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain).
Rearrange: lateral strain = sigma * longitudinal strain.
Substitute: lateral strain = 0.5 * 0.02.
The lateral strain is opposite in sign (the wire thins when stretched), magnitude 0.01.
This matches option C.
questions.info: Poisson's ratio is a pure number; for most materials it lies between 0 and 0.5, and 0.5 is the theoretical maximum (incompressible material).
questions.trick: Lateral strain = half of longitudinal strain when sigma = 0.5; just halve 0.02.

questions.q: The depth of ocean is 5000 m. Calculate the pressure exerted by water at the bottom of the ocean (take g = 10 m s^-2).
questions.given: h = 5000 m, g = 10 m/s^2, density of water = 1000 kg/m^3.
questions.concept: Hydrostatic pressure due to a liquid column is P = h*rho*g.
calculation: Formula: P = h * rho * g (pressure due to water alone).
Density of water rho = 1000 kg/m^3.
This matches option D.
questions.info: Total (absolute) pressure adds atmospheric pressure (about 10^5 Pa), which is negligible here compared to 5*10^7 Pa.
questions.trick: Every 10 m of water adds about 1 atm (10^5 Pa): 5000 m gives 500 atm = 5*10^7 Pa.

questions.q: Which statement is INCORRECT about heat?
options: Two bodies at the same temperature can have different heat contents
Heat content depends on mass, temperature and nature
When mixed, total heat = sum of individual heat contents
questions.given: Four statements about a body's 'heat content' - need to identify the one that is INCORRECT.
questions.concept: Heat is energy in transit between bodies due to a temperature difference - it is not a property a body 'contains' (unlike internal energy), so a body does not strictly have a fixed, storable 'heat content'.
calculation: Idea: heat is energy in transit due to a temperature difference. A body does not 'store' heat. It stores internal energy. We test each option.
Option B: calorimetry is the method used to measure heat exchanged. This is correct, so B is not the answer.
Option C: heat absorbed Q = m*c*(change in T) depends on mass, temperature change and nature (specific heat). Treated as correct, so C is not the answer.
Option D: on mixing, heat lost by hot body = heat gained by cold body, so total is the sum of parts. This is the calorimetry principle. Correct, so D is not the answer.
Option A: it says bodies at the same temperature can hold different heat contents. This treats heat as something a body contains, which is wrong, since heat is only energy in transit.
So A is the INCORRECT statement.
questions.info: Don't confuse heat (energy transferred due to a temperature difference, path-dependent) with internal energy (a state property) or temperature (a measure of average molecular kinetic energy) - this mix-up is a very common trap in conceptual thermo MCQs.
questions.trick: Whenever an option says a body 'has' or 'contains' heat, flag it as suspicious - strictly only internal energy is 'contained'; heat is only ever something that flows or is exchanged.

questions.q: A diatomic molecule (rigid rotator) has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.given: Diatomic molecule, modelled as a rigid rotator (vibration ignored).
questions.concept: Degrees of freedom f = translational (3) + rotational (for a diatomic molecule, 2 independent rotation axes perpendicular to the bond, since spin about the bond axis itself is negligible).
calculation: Degrees of freedom f = number of independent ways a molecule can move and store energy.
Translation: a molecule can move along x, y and z. So translational f = 3.
Rotation: a diatomic molecule is a dumbbell along its bond axis. It can rotate about 2 axes perpendicular to the bond.
Rotation about the bond axis itself is negligible, because the atoms are points on that axis. So rotational f = 2.
Rigid rotator means no vibration, so vibrational f = 0.
Total f = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5.
questions.info: If vibration were allowed (non-rigid diatomic, at high temperature), 2 more vibrational degrees of freedom (1 kinetic + 1 potential) get added, giving f=7 - which is exactly why '7' is included as a trap option here.
questions.trick: For degrees-of-freedom MCQs just memorise the three standard cases: monatomic f=3, diatomic rigid f=5, diatomic with vibration f=7 - no need to re-derive each time.

questions.q: An ideal gas's pressure is halved in an isothermal process. Its RMS speed becomes n*v_rms. What is n?
questions.given: Isothermal process, gas pressure is halved, new rms speed = n * (old rms speed).
questions.concept: RMS speed of gas molecules: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), which depends only on temperature T and molar mass M, not on pressure.
calculation: Formula: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M). R is a constant, M is the molar mass of the gas, T is the temperature.
Isothermal means T is constant. The gas is the same, so M is constant.
Pressure P does not appear in the formula at all. So halving the pressure does not change v_rms.
Hence new v_rms = old v_rms, so n * v_rms = v_rms.
Divide both sides by v_rms: n = 1.
Check: sqrt2, 1/sqrt2 and 2 would need a change in T, which is not allowed here.
questions.info: This trips students up because P, V and v_rms are all linked via PV=nRT, but v_rms itself is tied only to temperature - changing P at constant T (by changing V) never changes v_rms.
questions.trick: Whenever a question says 'isothermal' and asks about rms speed, the answer is almost always 'unchanged' (n=1) - you can often answer the instant you spot the keyword 'isothermal', with no calculation needed.

questions.q: A body cools from 70C to 40C in 5 minutes (surroundings at 10C, Newton's law of cooling). How long to cool from 50C to 20C?
questions.given: Cools from 70C to 40C in 5 min with surroundings at 10C; find time to cool from 50C to 20C.
questions.concept: Newton's law of cooling (average-temperature form): (T1-T2)/t = k * (T_avg - T_surroundings), where T_avg = (T1+T2)/2.
calculation: Formula (Newton's law of cooling, average form): (T1 - T2)/t = k * (T_avg - T_s), where T_avg = (T1 + T2)/2 and T_s = 10 C.
Cross-multiply: t = 30 x 3/10 = 9 minutes.
questions.info: Newton's law of cooling is only accurate for small temperature differences from the surroundings; using the average temperature per interval is the standard approximation taught at this level (the exact calculus form is dT/dt = -k(T-Ts)).
questions.trick: Set up both cases as (DeltaT/t) = k*(T_avg - T_surroundings), solve for k using the first case, then reuse that same k in the second case - no need to worry about k's actual units, just treat it as a ratio.

questions.q: The temperature in Fahrenheit scale is 77 F. Calculate the temperature in C.
questions.concept: Celsius and Fahrenheit are related by (C)/(5) = (F - 32)/(9).
calculation: Formula: C/5 = (F - 32)/9.
Substitute F = 77: C/5 = (77 - 32)/9.
C = 25. Matches option D.
questions.info: Both scales agree at -40 degrees (-40 C = -40 F). Water freezes at 32 F and boils at 212 F.
questions.trick: Subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9: (45 * 5)/9 = 25.

questions.q: A pendulum's length is increased by 10%. Its time period increases by about:
questions.given: Simple pendulum length L increased by 10%; find approximate % increase in time period T.
questions.concept: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), so T is proportional to sqrt(L); for small changes, fractional change in T is half the fractional change in L.
calculation: Formula: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). So T is proportional to sqrt(L), meaning T is proportional to L^(1/2).
New length L' = L + 10% of L = 1.1 L.
New period T' = 2*pi*sqrt(1.1 L/g) = sqrt(1.1) x T.
Increase = 0.0488 = 4.88 percent, which is about 5 percent.
Quick exam method: for small changes, percent change in T = (1/2) x percent change in L = (1/2) x 10 = 5 percent.
questions.info: This 'half the percentage change' rule applies to any relation of the form T proportional to L^n (in general %change in T ~ n * %change in L) - the same trick works for orbital period vs orbital radius problems too.
questions.trick: For 'quantity varies as square root of X, X changes by a small %' questions, just halve the percentage change directly instead of recomputing the new T and comparing - much faster under exam time pressure.

questions.q: SHM: x(t)=2.0*sin(40t) metres. Find the maximum velocity.
questions.given: SHM displacement x(t) = 2.0*sin(40t), x in metres, t in seconds.
questions.concept: For x(t) = A*sin(omega*t), velocity v(t) = dx/dt = A*omega*cos(omega*t), so maximum speed = A*omega.
calculation: Standard SHM form: x = A*sin(omega*t). Compare with x = 2.0*sin(40t).
So amplitude A = 2.0 m and angular frequency omega = 40 rad/s.
Velocity is the derivative of x: v = dx/dt = A*omega*cos(omega*t).
Substitute: v = 2.0 x 40 x cos(40t) = 80*cos(40t).
The largest value of cos(40t) is 1, so v_max = 80 x 1 = 80 m/s.
Check: option D, 80*cos(40t), is velocity at time t, not the maximum. The maximum is the number 80.
questions.info: Maximum speed in SHM always occurs at the mean position (x=0), while maximum acceleration occurs at the extreme positions (x=+-A) - a useful complementary fact.
questions.trick: For SHM max-velocity questions, just multiply amplitude by angular frequency (v_max = A*omega) read directly off the given x(t) - no need to actually differentiate term by term.

questions.q: Using SONAR, a source of ultrasonic waves of frequency 0.06 MHz sends down a pulse towards the seabed, which returns after 0.80 s. If the speed of sound in sea water is 1700 m/s, the depth of sea and the wavelength of the pulse respectively are:
questions.given: f = 0.06 MHz = 6*10^4 Hz, round-trip time t = 0.80 s, v = 1700 m/s.
questions.concept: Echo covers twice the depth: 2d = v*t. Wavelength = v/f.
calculation: Formula: pulse goes down and back, so 2d = v*t. Wavelength lambda = v/f.
Distance travelled = 1700 * 0.80 = 1360 m.
Depth 680 m and wavelength 0.0283 m, which is option B.
questions.info: SONAR stands for SOund NAvigation and Ranging. Ultrasonic waves are used as they have short wavelength, so they form narrow, directional beams.
questions.trick: Never forget the halving: echo time covers to-and-fro, so depth = v*t/2.

questions.q: The longest wavelength of the ultrasonic waves in air at room temperature is nearly:
questions.given: Ultrasonic means frequency above 20 kHz; speed of sound in air about 340 m/s.
questions.concept: Wavelength = v/f; longest wavelength corresponds to the lowest ultrasonic frequency, 20 kHz.
calculation: Formula: lambda = v/f.
Ultrasonic waves have frequency above 20 kHz, so the longest wavelength comes from f = 20,000 Hz.
Take v = 340 m/s in air at room temperature.
0.017 m = 17 mm, which is option C.
questions.info: Audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Below 20 Hz is infrasonic, above 20 kHz is ultrasonic.
questions.trick: Remember 340/20000 = 17 mm: the longest ultrasonic wavelength in air.

questions.q: The equation of SHM is y = a sin(3 pi n t + alpha). Then its phase at time t is:
questions.given: y = a sin(3*pi*n*t + alpha).
questions.concept: In y = a sin(omega*t + phi), the whole argument of sine is the phase.
calculation: Compare with the standard SHM form y = a sin(omega*t + phi).
Here omega = 3*pi*n and the initial phase phi = alpha.
The phase at time t is the entire angle inside the sine.
Phase = omega*t + phi = 3*pi*n*t + alpha.
Options A, B and C do not contain this expression.
So the answer is option D.
questions.info: Phase at t = 0 is called the initial phase or epoch (here alpha). Phase changes by 2*pi after one full time period.
questions.trick: Phase = whole bracket of sine or cosine; do not confuse it with just the phase constant alpha.

questions.q: A tuning fork makes 220 vibrations per second in air. When the velocity of sound is 330 m/s, the wavelength of tone emitted is:
questions.given: Frequency f = 220 Hz, speed v = 330 m/s.
questions.concept: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
calculation: Formula: v = f * lambda, so lambda = v/f.
Substitute: lambda = 330/220.
Divide both by 110: 330/220 = 3/2.
lambda = 1.5 m.
This matches option B.
questions.info: Frequency of a wave depends only on the source; when sound enters another medium its speed and wavelength change but the frequency stays the same.
questions.trick: Simplify the ratio by 110 first: 330/220 = 3/2 = 1.5.

questions.q: Charges q and -2q placed 6m apart on a horizontal plane. What is the locus of zero potential?
questions.given: Point charge q and point charge -2q, 6m apart on a line.
questions.concept: Zero-potential locus: V = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(q1/r1 + q2/r2) = 0, giving r2 = 2*r1 (an Apollonius circle, not a straight line, since |q1| != |q2|).
calculation: Put q at A = (0,0) and -2q at B = (6,0). Let P be a point with distances r1 from A and r2 from B.
Potential at P: V = k*q/r1 + k*(-2q)/r2 = 0.
So q/r1 = 2q/r2. Cross-multiply: r2 = 2*r1. P is twice as far from B as from A.
Point on line AB between A and B at (x,0): r1 = x, r2 = 6 - x. So 6 - x = 2x, 3x = 6, x = 2. Point (2,0).
Point on the line on the far side of A, at (-d,0): r1 = d, r2 = 6 + d. So 6 + d = 2d, d = 6. Point (-6,0).
These two points lie on the locus and are opposite ends of a diameter of the circle.
Diameter = 2 - (-6) = 8 m, so radius = 8/2 = 4 m.
Centre = midpoint = (2 + (-6))/2 = -2, so centre (-2,0). Circle of radius 4 m, centre (-2,0).
questions.info: For any two unlike charges, the zero-potential surface is always a circle (never a plane/line) unless |q1|=|q2|, in which case it becomes the perpendicular bisector.
questions.trick: Use the section-formula shortcut: find the points dividing the line joining the charges internally and externally in the ratio |q1|:|q2| - those two points are the diameter ends of the zero-potential circle.

questions.q: What is the electric field intensity at point P due to a short dipole, placed in air/vacuum?
questions.given: Short dipole, moment p, field point P on the axial line at distance r from the dipole's centre.
questions.concept: Axial field of a short dipole: E = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(2p/r^3), directed along the dipole axis.
calculation: Model the dipole as +q and -q separated by 2a. Dipole moment p = q x 2a. Field point P is on the axis at distance r from the centre.
Distance of P from +q is (r - a). Distance of P from -q is (r + a).
P is nearer +q, so the field of +q is bigger. Field of +q points away from +q. Field of -q points towards -q, which is the opposite way. So they subtract: E = kq/(r-a)^2 - kq/(r+a)^2.
Take common denominator: E = kq * [(r+a)^2 - (r-a)^2] / (r^2 - a^2)^2.
Numerator: (r+a)^2 - (r-a)^2 = 4ar. So E = kq*4ar/(r^2 - a^2)^2.
Short dipole means a is much smaller than r, so r^2 - a^2 is about r^2. Then E = kq*4ar/r^4 = 4kqa/r^3.
Write 4qa = 2 x (q x 2a) = 2p. So E = 2kp/r^3, with k = 1/(4*pi*eps0).
E = (1/(4*pi*eps0)) x (2p/r^3). The cube in r^3 rules out options A and B. In air or vacuum K = 1, so no K term, which rules out D.
questions.info: The equatorial (broadside-on) field of the same dipole is exactly half this value and points opposite to p: E_eq = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(p/r^3) - a common MCQ trap.
questions.trick: The factor of '2' belongs only to the axial field; if a question instead says 'equatorial' or 'perpendicular bisector', drop the 2.

questions.q: A long wire (charge/length lambda) is surrounded by a hollow cylinder (net charge/length 2*lambda). Find the field outside the cylinder, distance r from axis.
questions.given: Long wire with linear charge density lambda, coaxial hollow cylinder with net linear charge density 2*lambda; find field outside the cylinder at distance r.
questions.concept: Gauss's law for cylindrical symmetry: E*(2*pi*r*L) = Q_enclosed/eps0.
calculation: Formula (Gauss's law): E x (area of Gaussian surface) = Q_enclosed / eps0.
Take a coaxial cylinder of radius r (outside the hollow cylinder) and length L as the Gaussian surface.
Curved area = 2*pi*r*L. Flat ends add no flux, since the field is radial.
Charge on the wire inside = lambda x L. Charge on the hollow cylinder inside = 2*lambda x L.
Q_enclosed = lambda*L + 2*lambda*L = 3*lambda*L.
E x 2*pi*r*L = 3*lambda*L/eps0. Cancel L from both sides.
E = 3*lambda/(2*pi*eps0*r).
Net charge is positive, so field points radially outward. Matches option C.
questions.info: Between the wire and the cylinder's wall, the field would come from the wire alone (lambda/(2*pi*eps0*r)) - the cylinder's charge only adds in once your Gaussian surface is outside it.
questions.trick: For coaxial charge systems, just add up all the linear charge densities enclosed by your Gaussian surface - the exact shape (wire vs shell) doesn't matter, only enclosed charge does.

questions.q: A mass m (charge -q1) moves around a fixed charge +q2 in a circular path (radius r). What is the period of revolution T?
questions.given: Charge -q1, mass m, orbits fixed charge +q2 in a circle of radius r; find period T.
questions.concept: Coulomb attraction supplies centripetal force: k*q1*q2/r^2 = m*omega^2*r, with omega = 2*pi/T.
calculation: The charge moves in a circle, so the Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force.
Formula: k*q1*q2/r^2 = m*omega^2*r, where omega = 2*pi/T.
Substitute omega: k*q1*q2/r^2 = m*(4*pi^2/T^2)*r.
Multiply both sides by r^2 and T^2: k*q1*q2*T^2 = 4*pi^2*m*r^3.
Put k = 1/(4*pi*eps0), so 1/k = 4*pi*eps0.
Take square root: T = sqrt(16*pi^3*eps0*m*r^3/(q1*q2)).
questions.info: This is the electrostatic analogue of Kepler's third law (T^2 proportional to r^3) - identical algebra to gravitational orbits, just replace GMm with q1*q2/(4*pi*eps0).
questions.trick: Recognise the Kepler-style pattern instantly for any inverse-square central force giving circular motion - you only need to track which constants replace GM to pick the right option fast.

questions.q: Fields E1=14 V/m and E2=18 V/m on either side of a charged plate. What is the charge density on the plate (in terms of eps0)?
questions.given: Fields E1=14 V/m and E2=18 V/m on the two sides of a charged plate.
questions.concept: For a charged sheet (possibly in an external field), the fields on its two sides are E_ext -+ sigma/(2*eps0); their difference isolates the sheet's own charge: E2 - E1 = sigma/eps0.
calculation: A charged plate may sit in an outside field. The fields on its two sides are E_ext + sigma/(2*eps0) and E_ext - sigma/(2*eps0).
Subtract the smaller from the larger: E2 - E1 = [E_ext + sigma/(2*eps0)] - [E_ext - sigma/(2*eps0)] = sigma/eps0. The E_ext part cancels.
Formula: sigma = eps0 x (E2 - E1).
sigma = eps0 x 4 = 4*eps0.
This matches option A.
questions.info: If the two fields had come out equal, that would mean the plate carries zero net charge (sigma=0) - a handy sanity check for this type of problem.
questions.trick: Don't solve for the external field separately - surface charge density only needs the DIFFERENCE of the two given fields, so just subtract and multiply by eps0.

questions.q: A point charge Q is on the axis of a disk (radius R), distance h from the disk's plane. If 1/4 of the electric flux passes through the disk, what is R (in terms of a distance variable b)?
questions.given: Point charge Q on the axis of a disk of radius R, at axial distance (given as h in the question, called b in the options); 1/4 of total flux passes through the disk.
questions.concept: Flux through a disk subtending half-angle theta at the charge: phi = (Q/2*eps0)*(1 - cos(theta)); total flux from the charge = Q/eps0.
calculation: Flux from a point charge through a disk on its axis: phi = (Q/(2*eps0)) x (1 - cos(theta)). Here theta is the half-angle the disk makes at the charge.
Total flux from the charge is Q/eps0. One fourth of it is (1/4) x Q/eps0 = Q/(4*eps0).
Set equal: (Q/(2*eps0)) x (1 - cos(theta)) = Q/(4*eps0).
Cancel Q/eps0 from both sides: (1/2)(1 - cos(theta)) = 1/4.
Multiply by 2: 1 - cos(theta) = 1/2, so cos(theta) = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees.
In the right triangle formed by the axis (length b), the disk radius R and the slant line: tan(theta) = R/b.
R = b x tan(60) = sqrt3 x b.
questions.info: The flux-through-a-cap formula phi = (Q/2*eps0)*(1-cos(theta)) is the same geometry used in 'flux through one face of a cube with a charge at a corner' problems - worth memorising once and reusing.
questions.trick: A given fraction of total flux converts directly to cos(theta): here 1/4 of total flux gives cos(theta)=1/2, i.e. the standard 60-degree angle, after which it's just tan(60)=sqrt3 to get R in terms of b.

questions.q: The electric field E at distance r from an infinitely long straight wire (uniform charge density lambda) satisfies, for a given lambda:
questions.given: Field at distance r from an infinite line charge of linear density lambda.
questions.concept: Gauss's law with a cylindrical Gaussian surface: E*(2*pi*r*L) = lambda*L/eps0.
calculation: Formula (Gauss's law): E x (area) = Q_enclosed/eps0.
Take a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L. Curved area = 2*pi*r*L. Flat ends give no flux.
Charge enclosed = lambda x L.
E x 2*pi*r*L = lambda*L/eps0. Cancel L.
E = lambda/(2*pi*eps0*r).
For a given lambda, 2*pi*eps0 and lambda are constants, so E is proportional to 1/r. Option B.
questions.info: Contrast the three standard Gauss's-law geometries: point charge gives E proportional to 1/r^2, line charge gives 1/r, and an infinite charged plane gives a CONSTANT field (independent of r) - a favourite thing exams test.
questions.trick: Just memorise the three r-dependences (point: 1/r^2, line: 1/r, plane: constant) instead of re-deriving Gauss's law each time.

questions.q: A rectangular area (4.0cm x 5.0cm) in field E=(4.0x10^2 N/C)i, with normal unit vector [(1/2)i+(sqrt3/2)j]. What is the electric flux through the rectangle?
questions.given: Area 4.0cm x 5.0cm, field E=(4.0x10^2 N/C)i, unit normal n = (1/2)i + (sqrt3/2)j.
questions.concept: Electric flux phi = E (dot) A, where vector A = (area)*n_hat.
calculation: Formula: flux = E dot A, where vector A = (area) x n_hat.
E = 4.0 x 10^2 i (no j part). n_hat = (1/2) i + (sqrt3/2) j.
Dot product: E dot n_hat = (4.0 x 10^2)(1/2) + (0)(sqrt3/2) = 2.0 x 10^2 N/C. Only i parts multiply.
Flux = (E dot n_hat) x area = 2.0 x 10^2 x 2.0 x 10^-3.
questions.info: Only the component of E along the normal contributes to flux - here the j-part of n_hat is irrelevant because E itself has zero j-component, which simplifies the dot product a lot.
questions.trick: Convert area to m^2 FIRST (cm^2 to m^2 needs x10^-4, a common slip), then take the dot product of E with the unit normal before multiplying by area.

questions.q: Charges A(-0.144nC) at (-16cm,0) and B(0.256nC) at (0,12cm). Find the field magnitude at (-16cm,12cm).
questions.given: qA=-0.144nC at (-16cm,0); qB=0.256nC at (0,12cm); find field magnitude at (-16cm,12cm).
questions.concept: Superposition: E_net = E_A + E_B, each from Coulomb's law E=kq/r^2, each directed along the line from its charge to the field point.
calculation: Let P = (-16 cm, 12 cm). Use E = k*q/r^2 with k = 9 x 10^9 and add the two fields as vectors.
A is at (-16, 0). P is directly above A, so r_A = 12 cm = 0.12 m.
E_A = 9 x 10^9 x 0.144 x 10^-9 / (0.12)^2 = 1.296 / 0.0144 = 90 N/C. A is negative, so this field points toward A, which is downward.
B is at (0, 12). P is directly to the left of B, so r_B = 16 cm = 0.16 m.
E_B = 9 x 10^9 x 0.256 x 10^-9 / (0.16)^2 = 2.304 / 0.0256 = 90 N/C. B is positive, so this field points away from B, which is to the left.
E_A is vertical and E_B is horizontal, so they are at 90 degrees.
E_net = 127.3 N/C, about 127 N/C.
questions.info: This is a scaled-down version of the classic NCERT worked example with the same 12-16-20 cm (3-4-5 scaled) right-triangle geometry, which is why the two perpendicular field contributions come out equal.
questions.trick: Spot the 12-16-20 right triangle (scaled 3-4-5) immediately - it tells you the two fields are perpendicular, so you can jump straight to sqrt(E_A^2+E_B^2) without computing any angles.

questions.q: Three equal +q charges at the vertices of an equilateral triangle (side l). Find the force on a charge Q (same sign) at the centroid.
questions.given: Three equal charges +q at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side l; test charge Q at the centroid.
questions.concept: By symmetry, three equal-magnitude forces directed at 120 degrees to each other sum to zero (standard vector identity).
calculation: Idea: use symmetry. The charge Q sits at the centroid, the same distance from all three corners.
Distance from centroid to each vertex d = l/sqrt3.
Each charge q pushes Q (same sign, so repulsion) with force F = k*q*Q/d^2. All three forces have the same size F.
The three forces point from each vertex towards the centroid and beyond. They make 120 degrees with each other.
Add two of them: two forces F at 120 degrees give a resultant of magnitude F, pointing opposite to the third force.
The third force F points the opposite way, so it cancels that resultant exactly.
Net force on Q = F - F = 0. Matches option D.
questions.info: This symmetry shortcut (equal charges equally spaced around a regular polygon give zero net force/field at the centre) is a very common NCERT/competitive-exam pattern that avoids any vector algebra.
questions.trick: Whenever equal charges sit with full rotational symmetry around a central point, answer 'zero' immediately - no need to resolve any components.

questions.q: Two charges q_1 and q_2 are placed on the x-axis, with q_1 at x = a, and q_2 at x = 3a. A third charge Q is placed at the origin. The net force on charge Q is zero if q_2 is equal to:
questions.given: q_1 at x = a, q_2 at x = 3a, Q at origin; net force on Q is zero.
questions.concept: Coulomb's law: for zero net force the two forces on Q must be equal and opposite.
calculation: Formula (Coulomb's law): F = k*Q*q/r^2.
Force on Q due to q_1 (distance a): F_1 = k*Q*q_1/a^2.
Force on Q due to q_2 (distance 3a): F_2 = k*Q*q_2/(3a)^2 = k*Q*q_2/(9a^2).
Both charges lie on the same side of Q, so for zero net force F_1 and F_2 must point in opposite directions with equal size.
Magnitudes equal: k*Q*q_1/a^2 = k*Q*|q_2|/(9a^2).
Cancel k, Q and a^2: q_1 = |q_2|/9, so |q_2| = 9*q_1.
Opposite directions means q_1 and q_2 have opposite signs, so q_2 = -9*q_1. Matches option D.
questions.info: The distance ratio is 3, so the force ratio is 3^2 = 9; this is why the magnitude is 9 and not 3.
questions.trick: Charges on the same side of Q need opposite signs; magnitude = q_1 x (distance ratio)^2.

questions.q: An electric dipole of dipole moment p is placed in an electric field E. The torque exerted by the field on the dipole is:
options: parallel to both the field and the dipole moment
perpendicular to both the field and the dipole moment
parallel to the field and perpendicular to the dipole moment
parallel to dipole moment and perpendicular to the field.
questions.given: Dipole moment p in field E; find direction of torque.
questions.concept: Torque on a dipole is the cross product p x E, so it is perpendicular to both p and E.
calculation: Formula: torque = p x E (vector cross product).
A cross product of two vectors is always perpendicular to the plane containing both vectors.
So the torque is perpendicular to p and also perpendicular to E.
Its magnitude is p*E*sin(theta), where theta is the angle between p and E.
Torque is zero only when p is parallel or antiparallel to E, so it cannot be parallel to either in general.
Options A, C and D each say the torque is parallel to p or E, which is not possible for a cross product. Matches option B.
questions.info: The torque tends to rotate p towards E; at theta = 90 degrees the torque is maximum (p*E).
questions.trick: Torque = p x E, any cross product is perpendicular to both vectors.

questions.q: A 5.0 microC charge is placed at the centre of a Gaussian surface in the form of a cube. The electric flux through any one face of the cube is:
questions.given: q = 5.0 microC = 5*10^-6 C at the centre of a cube; flux through one face.
questions.concept: Gauss's law: total flux = q/eps0; by symmetry each of the 6 faces gets one-sixth.
calculation: Formula (Gauss's law): total flux = q/eps0, eps0 = 8.85*10^-12.
The charge is at the centre, so the flux divides equally among 6 faces by symmetry.
Flux per face = (5.65*10^5)/6.
Flux per face = 0.94*10^5 = 9.4*10^4 N m^2/C. Matches option C.
questions.info: Using 1/(4*pi*eps0) = 9*10^9, flux per face = 4*pi*k*q/6 which gives the same value.
questions.trick: Total flux for 1 microC is about 1.13*10^5; multiply by q and divide by 6 for a cube.

questions.q: Two point charges, +3.0 microC and +8.0 microC are separated by 0.30 m. The potential energy of this two charge system, relative to potential energy at infinite separation, is:
questions.concept: Electrostatic potential energy of two point charges: U = k*q_1*q_2/r.
calculation: Formula: U = k*q_1*q_2/r with k = 9*10^9 N m^2/C^2.
Divide by r: U = 0.216/0.30.
U = 0.72 J. Matches option D.
questions.info: U is positive for like charges (work must be done to bring them together) and negative for unlike charges.
questions.trick: Do k*q_1*q_2 first (9*24 = 216, powers give 10^-3), then divide by r.

questions.q: Two capacitors with capacitances 2.0 microF and 1.0 microF, respectively, are connected in parallel. The system is connected to a 100 V battery. The charge on the 2.0 microF capacitor is:
questions.given: C_1 = 2.0 microF, C_2 = 1.0 microF in parallel, V = 100 V; find charge on C_1.
questions.concept: In parallel each capacitor has the full battery voltage, so Q = C*V for each.
calculation: Formula: Q = C*V.
In a parallel combination the voltage across each capacitor equals the battery voltage, 100 V.
Charge on the 2.0 microF capacitor: Q = 2.0*10^-6 x 100.
Q = 200*10^-6 C = 200 microC. Matches option B.
Check: the 1.0 microF capacitor holds 100 microC and the total is 300 microC, which is option A (the total charge, not the asked one).
questions.info: In parallel the charge divides in the ratio of capacitances; in series the charge is the same on all.
questions.trick: Parallel: same V, so Q = C*V directly; do not use the total charge.

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates, has a capacitance of 2 pF. The plate separation is doubled and a dielectric slab is inserted so that it completely fills the space between the plates. The capacitance of the capacitor becomes 4 pF. The dielectric constant of the slab is:
questions.given: C_air = 2 pF; separation becomes 2d; with dielectric C = 4 pF; find K.
questions.concept: Parallel plate capacitor: C = K*eps0*A/d, so C is proportional to K and inversely to d.
calculation: Formula: C = K*eps0*A/d.
Initially (air, K = 1): C_0 = eps0*A/d = 2 pF.
After the change: C = K*eps0*A/(2d) = (K/2) x (eps0*A/d).
So C = (K/2) x C_0 = (K/2) x 2 pF = K pF.
Given C = 4 pF, so K = 4.
Dielectric constant = 4.0. Matches option C.
questions.info: Dielectric constant of any material is at least 1 (vacuum = 1), so options with K less than 1 can be rejected at once.
questions.trick: Doubling d halves C; the dielectric must then multiply C by K, so 2 x (1/2) x K = 4 gives K = 4.

questions.q: In a dielectric medium, the dielectric polarization P, electric displacement D and electric field E are related as:
questions.given: Relation among D, E and P inside a dielectric.
questions.concept: Electric displacement D = eps0*E + P, where P is the dipole moment per unit volume.
calculation: Formula: D = eps0*E + P.
D is electric displacement, E is the electric field and P is the polarization (dipole moment per unit volume).
Check options A and B: they place D and P on the wrong sides, so they fail.
Option D has a negative sign on eps0*E, which is wrong.
Option C matches D = eps0*E + P.
questions.info: For a linear dielectric P = eps0*chi*E, so D = eps0*(1 + chi)*E = eps0*K*E, where K is the dielectric constant.
questions.trick: In vacuum P = 0 so D = eps0*E. The correct relation must reduce to this, which only option C does.

questions.q: A body has -70 micro-Coulomb of charge. The number of additional electrons in it will be (charge of electron e = -1.6 * 10^-19):
questions.given: Q = -70 micro-C = -70*10^-6 C, e = 1.6*10^-19 C in magnitude.
questions.concept: Charge is quantised: Q = n*e, so n = Q/e.
calculation: Formula: Q = n*e, so n = Q/e.
Q = 70 micro-C = 70 * 10^-6 = 7*10^-5 C (magnitude).
n = 4.375*10^14, which is closest to 4.3*10^14 among the options (the paper keys it as 4.3*10^14). Matches option C.
questions.info: Charge is quantised in units of e = 1.6*10^-19 C; a negative body has an excess of electrons, a positive body has a deficit.
questions.trick: Mantissa 7/1.6 is a little above 4: only option C (4.3) fits; power is 10^(19 - 5) = 10^14.

questions.q: A galvanometer (20 ohm, full-scale at 2mA) needs converting to a 0-6A ammeter. What shunt is needed?
options: A 6.66 milliohm shunt resistor, connected in parallel with the galvanometer
questions.given: Galvanometer G=20 ohm, full-scale deflection current Ig=2mA; required ammeter range I=0 to 6A.
questions.concept: Shunt conversion: Ig*G = (I-Ig)*S, where shunt S is placed in PARALLEL with the galvanometer to bypass the excess current.
calculation: A shunt is a small resistance S in parallel with the galvanometer. It carries the extra current, so the meter reads a larger range.
Formula: Ig x G = (I - Ig) x S. The galvanometer and shunt have the same voltage across them.
Ig = 2 mA = 0.002 A, G = 20 ohm, I = 6 A.
I - Ig = 6 - 0.002 = 5.998 A, which is about 6 A.
S = 0.04 / 5.998 = 0.00667 ohm = 6.67 milliohm. The closest option is 6.66 milliohm.
Connection: parallel, never series. Series would add resistance and not extend the range. Only option A has parallel with about 6.66 milliohm.
questions.info: The shunt's main job is to protect the sensitive galvanometer coil by carrying almost all of the large current, while only the tiny Ig actually flows through the meter movement.
questions.trick: Just plug into S = Ig*G/(I-Ig) directly and immediately eliminate any option that says 'series', since a shunt must be parallel by definition.

questions.q: An alloy made of metals A and B has resistivity R_alloy. Which relation holds true (compared to the pure metals' resistivities R_A, R_B)?
questions.given: Alloy of metals A and B has resistivity R_alloy; compare with pure metal resistivities R_A and R_B.
questions.concept: Alloying disrupts the regular crystal lattice of either pure metal, increasing electron scattering and hence resistivity above both pure constituents.
calculation: Resistivity depends on how much conduction electrons are scattered while moving through the metal.
A pure metal has atoms in a regular, ordered lattice. Electrons scatter little.
In an alloy, atoms of A and B are mixed randomly. This breaks the regular lattice.
So electrons scatter more than in either pure metal.
More scattering means higher resistivity: R_alloy is greater than R_A and also greater than R_B.
Check: options with R_alloy less than R_A or less than R_B fail. Only option C has both greater than.
questions.info: This is exactly why practical resistance wires (manganin, constantan, nichrome) are alloys, not pure metals - they give higher resistivity plus a very low temperature coefficient of resistance, ideal for standard resistors and heaters.
questions.trick: No arithmetic needed - just remember the standalone NCERT fact 'alloy resistivity exceeds both parent metals' and pick that option directly.

questions.q: Two resistors (ratio 3:5) combine in series for an equivalent resistance of 24 ohms. Find R1 and R2.
questions.given: R1:R2 = 3:5, resistors in series, Rs = 24 ohm.
questions.concept: Series equivalent resistance: Rs = R1 + R2; express both resistors as parts of the given ratio.
calculation: Formula: series resistance Rs = R1 + R2.
Ratio R1 : R2 = 3 : 5, so let R1 = 3x and R2 = 5x.
Substitute: 3x + 5x = 24, so 8x = 24.
Divide both sides by 8: x = 3 ohm.
R1 = 3 x 3 = 9 ohm. R2 = 5 x 3 = 15 ohm.
Check: 9 + 15 = 24 ohm, and 9 : 15 = 3 : 5. Order matters: the 3 part is R1, so R1 = 9 and R2 = 15. Not 15 and 9.
questions.info: In a series combination the current through both resistors is identical, so the voltage drop splits in the same 3:5 ratio as the resistances.
questions.trick: Turn any 'ratio + total' resistor problem into parts (3x, 5x, etc.), sum to the given total, solve for x - works instantly for series ratio questions.

questions.q: A potentiometer: a 2.25V cell balances at 63.0cm; replaced by another cell, balance shifts to 21.0cm. Find the second cell's EMF.
questions.given: Cell 1: EMF=2.25V, balance length l1=63.0cm. Cell 2 (unknown EMF) balances at l2=21.0cm on the same wire.
questions.concept: Potentiometer balancing: EMF is proportional to balancing length since the potential gradient along the wire is constant, so E1/l1 = E2/l2.
calculation: Formula: on a potentiometer wire the potential gradient is constant, so EMF is proportional to balance length. E1/l1 = E2/l2.
Rearrange: E2 = E1 x (l2/l1).
questions.info: A potentiometer measures EMF with zero current drawn at balance, which is why it's more accurate than a voltmeter, which always draws some current and loads the circuit.
questions.trick: Spot that 21/63 simplifies cleanly to 1/3 - recognising easy ratios like this saves time over doing long division under exam pressure.

questions.q: Two cells (EMF e1,e2; internal resistance r1,r2) connected in parallel (like terminals together). Find the equivalent single-cell EMF.
questions.given: Two cells, EMFs e1 and e2, internal resistances r1 and r2, connected in parallel (like terminals joined together).
questions.concept: Equivalent EMF of parallel cells: model each cell as EMF with series internal resistance, apply node equation at the common junction to get Eeq = (e1*r2 + e2*r1)/(r1+r2).
calculation: Method: replace each cell by its EMF with a series internal resistance, then combine the two branches in parallel.
Each cell can be treated as a current source of strength e/r with a resistance r in parallel. So current sources: e1/r1 and e2/r2.
Parallel: currents add, so total I = e1/r1 + e2/r2. Conductances add, so 1/r_eq = 1/r1 + 1/r2.
Equivalent EMF = I x r_eq, so Eeq = (e1/r1 + e2/r2) / (1/r1 + 1/r2).
Multiply numerator and denominator by r1*r2 to clear the fractions.
Numerator: (e1/r1 + e2/r2) x r1*r2 = e1*r2 + e2*r1. Denominator: (1/r1 + 1/r2) x r1*r2 = r2 + r1.
Check: if r1 = r2 and e1 = e2, this gives e, which is correct for identical cells in parallel. Matches option B.
questions.info: This is a weighted average of the two EMFs, weighted by the OTHER cell's internal resistance - a cell with lower internal resistance pulls the equivalent EMF closer to its own value.
questions.trick: Memorise the final cross-pattern directly: each EMF pairs with the OTHER cell's resistance in the numerator, over the sum of resistances - instant recognition for parallel-cell EMF MCQs.

questions.q: The current in an electron beam in a cathode-ray tube is measured to be 80 microA. The number of electrons that hit the screen in 8 s is:
questions.concept: Current is charge per unit time: I = q/t = n*e/t.
calculation: Formula: I = q/t, and q = n*e.
Number of electrons: n = q/e = (6.4*10^-4)/(1.6*10^-19).
n = 4*10^15. Matches option C.
questions.info: Number of electrons per second for 1 A is 1/(1.6*10^-19) = 6.25*10^18.
questions.trick: Do 6.4/1.6 = 4 first, then fix the power: 10^-4 / 10^-19 = 10^15.

questions.q: A wire, 1.2 mm in diameter and 32 cm long, carries a current of 648 mA. The density of free electrons in the wire is 5.90 x 10^28 m^-3. The drift velocity of electrons in the wire is:
questions.concept: Drift velocity from I = n*A*e*v_d, so v_d = I/(n*A*e).
calculation: Formula: I = n*A*e*v_d, so v_d = I/(n*A*e).
v_d = 6.1*10^-5 m/s. Matches option B.
The length 32 cm is not needed; it is extra data.
questions.info: Drift velocity in metals is tiny (about 10^-4 m/s) even though the signal travels near light speed.
questions.trick: Ignore the length; use v_d = I/(n*A*e) and remember radius is half the diameter.

questions.q: Three resistors having individual resistance of 4.0 ohm, 6.0 ohm and 12.0 ohm, respectively are connected in parallel. This combination is connected in series with a 2.0 ohm resistor and a 12.0 V battery. The current in the 12 ohm resistor is:
questions.given: 4, 6, 12 ohm in parallel, in series with 2 ohm and a 12 V battery; find current in the 12 ohm resistor.
questions.concept: Parallel resistance via reciprocals, then Ohm's law; parallel resistors share the same voltage.
calculation: So R_p = 2 ohm.
Total resistance = R_p + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4 ohm.
Total current I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.
Voltage across the parallel part = I x R_p = 3 x 2 = 6 V.
Current in the 12 ohm resistor = 6/12 = 0.5 A. Matches option A.
Option D (3 A) is the total current, not the branch current.
questions.info: Parallel resistors share the same voltage; the current in each branch is inversely proportional to its resistance.
questions.trick: Find R_p first, then the voltage across it, then divide by the asked resistor.

questions.q: A battery with internal resistance r is connected in series with an external resistance R. Let U_r and U_R represent the energy dissipated per unit time by the internal resistance r and external resistance R, respectively. If r=R, then the ratio U_r/U_R is:
questions.given: Internal resistance r in series with external R; r = R; find power ratio U_r/U_R.
questions.concept: Series elements carry the same current, so power I^2*R is proportional to resistance.
calculation: Formula: power dissipated P = I^2 x resistance.
r and R are in series, so the same current I flows through both.
U_r = I^2*r and U_R = I^2*R.
Ratio U_r/U_R = (I^2*r)/(I^2*R) = r/R.
Given r = R, so the ratio = 1.
Matches option C.
questions.info: Maximum power is delivered to the load when R = r, and then exactly half of the battery power is wasted inside the battery (efficiency 50 percent).
questions.trick: In series, power divides in the ratio of resistances; equal resistances give ratio 1.

questions.q: A solenoid (5.0cm length, 0.40cm radius, 500 turns, 3.0A current). Find the magnetic field at the centre. (mu0/4pi=10^-7 T*m/A)
questions.given: Solenoid length L=5.0cm=0.05m, N=500 turns, I=3.0A (radius is irrelevant for the ideal solenoid field); mu0/4pi=10^-7.
questions.concept: Magnetic field inside a long solenoid: B = mu0*n*I, where n = N/L is the number of turns per unit length.
calculation: Formula: B = mu0 * n * I, where n = N/L is turns per metre. Radius is not needed for a long solenoid.
Convert length: L = 5.0 cm = 0.05 m.
Convert: 1 mT = 10^-3 T, so 0.0377 T = 37.7 mT, which is about 38 mT.
questions.info: The solenoid's cross-sectional radius doesn't appear in the ideal B=mu0*n*I formula at all - it's a classic distractor meant to tempt you into using the wrong variable.
questions.trick: Spot and discard irrelevant data (radius here) - solenoid field questions only ever need turns, length, and current.

questions.q: A 0.8cm current element (5A, +x direction) at the origin. Find the magnetic field at (0, 5cm).
questions.given: Current element: I=5A, dl=0.8cm=0.008m along +x axis at the origin; field point at (0, 0.05m, 0).
questions.concept: Biot-Savart law for a current element: dB = (mu0/4pi) * I*(dl-vector x r-hat)/r^2.
calculation: Formula (Biot-Savart): dB = (mu0/4pi) * I * dl * sin(angle) / r^2, direction from dl x r-hat.
Field point (0, 5 cm) lies on the +y axis from the origin, so r = 5 cm = 0.05 m and r-hat = j-hat.
Element is along +x, so dl x r-hat = dl * (i-hat x j-hat) = dl * k-hat. Angle is 90 degrees, so sin = 1.
Direction is +k-hat (positive z), so B = 1.6 microT k. This matches option A.
questions.info: Memorising i-hat x j-hat = k-hat lets you read off the field direction instantly instead of redrawing vector diagrams every time in these element-field problems.
questions.trick: When the field point lies exactly on the axis perpendicular to the current element, the angle between dl and r is 90 degrees, so sin(theta)=1 and you plug straight into mu0*I*dl/(4*pi*r^2) with no sine term needed.

questions.q: The energy required to build up current I in a coil of self-inductance L is:
questions.given: General case: energy required to build up current I in a coil of self-inductance L.
questions.concept: Energy stored in an inductor: W = (1/2)*L*I^2, found by integrating the instantaneous power delivered while current ramps up from 0 to I.
calculation: Idea: while current rises from 0 to I, the source must push charge against the self-induced EMF. That work is stored as energy.
