Induced EMF magnitude: e = L*(dI/dt).
Power at any instant: P = e * i = L * i * (di/dt).
Work in a small time dt: dW = P*dt = L * i * di.
Add up from i = 0 to i = I: W = integral of L*i di = L * [i^2/2] from 0 to I.
Check options: L*I and (1/2)*L*I do not have units of energy (joule). L*I^2 is missing the 1/2. Only (1/2)*L*I^2 is correct.
questions.info: This is the magnetic twin of a capacitor's (1/2)*C*V^2 - both represent energy stored in a field that's built up gradually as current or voltage ramps from zero.
questions.trick: Use the electrical/magnetic analogy: capacitor energy (1/2)CV^2 maps directly to inductor energy (1/2)LI^2 - knowing one instantly gives you the other's form.

questions.q: A 4.0A current in an 8.0mH inductor coil. What is the stored energy?
questions.given: I=4.0A, L=8.0mH=0.008H; find stored energy.
questions.concept: Energy stored in an inductor: W = (1/2)*L*I^2.
calculation: Formula: W = (1/2)*L*I^2.
Convert to mJ: 0.064 J = 0.064 * 1000 = 64 mJ.
questions.info: Energy scales with the SQUARE of the current, so doubling the current quadruples the stored energy - a common 'what if it doubled' follow-up twist in MCQs.
questions.trick: Convert mH to H by dividing by 1000 first, then apply W=0.5*L*I^2 directly - no need to go through EMF or flux at all.

questions.q: Current in one coil changes 0A to 10A in 0.5s; flux in a nearby coil changes by 40 Wb in that time. Find the mutual inductance.
questions.given: Coil 1 current changes from 0 to 10A in 0.5s (dI=10A); coil 2's flux changes by 40 Wb in that same time (dPhi=40 Wb).
questions.concept: Mutual inductance: M = dPhi2/dI1, the flux linked in coil 2 per unit change in coil 1's current.
calculation: Formula: M = (change in flux in coil 2) / (change in current in coil 1) = dPhi2 / dI1.
Change in current: dI1 = 10 - 0 = 10 A.
Change in flux: dPhi2 = 40 Wb.
Substitute: M = 40/10.
The 0.5 s time is not needed here, because the time cancels in the ratio. Do not divide by it.
questions.info: The 0.5s time interval is actually irrelevant here, since M=dPhi/dI doesn't need dt directly - time only matters if you were instead asked for the induced EMF.
questions.trick: Whenever a flux change and a current change are given together, go straight for M=dPhi/dI and ignore the stated time unless EMF is explicitly asked for.

questions.q: A constant current I is maintained in a pure-inductance coil L. The stored energy is:
questions.given: A constant (steady) current I is maintained in a coil of pure self-inductance L (no resistance).
questions.concept: Energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field: W = (1/2)*L*I^2, the same formula whether current is still rising or has settled to a steady value.
calculation: Formula: energy stored in a pure inductor W = (1/2)*L*I^2.
This formula depends only on L and the present current I. It does not depend on how fast the current was reached.
For steady current I, dI/dt = 0, so the induced EMF is 0 and no extra work is done. The stored energy stays fixed.
Check options: (1/4)*L*I^2 has a wrong factor. L*I^2 is missing the 1/2. L*I is not an energy (it is flux).
So stored energy W = (1/2)*L*I^2.
questions.info: In a pure (resistanceless) inductor carrying constant current, no power is dissipated and no extra energy is added - the (1/2)LI^2 just stays stored in the magnetic field indefinitely.
questions.trick: Any question phrased 'constant current maintained in pure inductance' is just testing whether you know the stored energy stays (1/2)LI^2 at steady state - don't overthink it with EMF equations.

questions.q: Two parallel conductors, each of 0.6 m length, separated by 6 mm carry equal currents of 4.0 A in opposite directions. The mutual force between the conductors is:
questions.given: L = 0.6 m, d = 6*10^-3 m, I_1 = I_2 = 4.0 A, opposite directions.
questions.concept: Force between parallel currents: F = mu0*I_1*I_2*L/(2*pi*d); opposite currents repel.
calculation: Formula: F = mu0*I_1*I_2*L/(2*pi*d), with mu0/(2*pi) = 2*10^-7 T m/A.
Currents are in opposite directions, so the force is repulsive.
Magnitude 3.2*10^-4 N, repulsive. Matches option D.
questions.info: Parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel (opposite to the rule for like and unlike charges).
questions.trick: Use mu0/(2*pi) = 2*10^-7 directly; opposite currents mean repulsion.

questions.q: A proton is moving at a speed of 3.8 x10^6 m/s in the positive x- direction. A magnetic field of 0.25x 10^-4 T is in the positive z- direction. The magnitude of the force acting on the proton is:
questions.concept: Magnetic force on a moving charge: F = q*v*B*sin(theta); here v is perpendicular to B.
calculation: Formula: F = q*v*B*sin(theta).
v is along x and B along z, so theta = 90 degrees and sin(theta) = 1.
F = 1.52*10^-17 N, about 1.5*10^-17 N. Matches option C.
questions.info: The direction of the force is along -y here (v x B for a positive charge: x cross z = -y); the force never changes the speed.
questions.trick: Perpendicular v and B give sin(theta) = 1; multiply the three numbers and add the powers.

questions.q: A solenoid with 400 turns is 10.0 cm long and has a radius of 1.0 cm. The current in the solenoid is 5A. The magnetic field at the centre of the solenoid is:
questions.given: N = 400, length = 10.0 cm = 0.10 m, radius 1.0 cm, I = 5 A.
questions.concept: Field inside a long solenoid: B = mu0*n*I, with n = N/length (turns per metre).
calculation: Formula: B = mu0*n*I, n = N/L.
n = 400/0.10 = 4000 turns per metre.
Length 10 cm is ten times the radius, so the solenoid is long enough for this formula.
B = 25.1*10^-3 = 2.5*10^-2 T. Matches option A.
questions.info: Field inside an ideal solenoid is uniform and independent of its radius; at an end it is half of the central value.
questions.trick: Compute n first (turns per metre in SI), then B = 4*pi*10^-7 x n x I, with 4*pi*10^-7 about 1.26*10^-6.

questions.q: The current in a coil with a self-inductance of 2.5 mH increases from 0 to 1.4 A in one-tenth of a second. The induced emf in the coil is:
questions.given: L = 2.5 mH = 2.5*10^-3 H, change in current = 1.4 A, time = 0.1 s.
questions.concept: Self-induced emf: emf = L*(dI/dt), magnitude only.
calculation: Formula: emf = L x (change in I)/(change in t).
Rate of change of current = 1.4/0.1 = 14 A/s.
emf = 35*10^-3 V = 35 mV. Matches option A.
questions.info: The induced emf opposes the change in current (Lenz's law), so it is negative in sign: emf = -L*dI/dt.
questions.trick: Convert mH to H first: 2.5 x 14 = 35, so the answer is 35 mV.

questions.q: A uniform magnetic field of 1.4 T passes through a wire loop of area 0.5 m^2. If the direction of the field makes a 30 degree angle with the normal to the plane of the loop, the magnetic flux through the loop is:
questions.given: B = 1.4 T, A = 0.5 m^2, angle between B and the normal = 30 degrees; find flux.
questions.concept: Magnetic flux = B*A*cos(theta), theta measured from the area normal.
calculation: Formula: flux = B x A x cos(theta), where theta is the angle between B and the normal to the loop.
Here theta = 30 degrees, so cos(30) = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866.
0.70 x 0.866 = 0.606, which is about 0.61 Wb.
This matches option C.
questions.info: Flux is maximum (B*A) when the field is along the normal (theta = 0) and zero when the field lies in the plane of the loop (theta = 90 degrees). Unit: 1 Wb = 1 T*m^2.
questions.trick: Check if the angle is given from the normal or from the plane. From the normal use cos, from the plane use sin.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements regarding magnetic materials is NOT correct?
options: Diamagnetic susceptibility is independent of temperature.
Ferromagnetic susceptibility is dependent on temperature.
Paramagnetic susceptibility is independent of temperature.
Paramagnetic susceptibility is dependent on temperature.
questions.given: Four statements on susceptibility versus temperature; pick the wrong one.
questions.concept: Curie's law: paramagnetic susceptibility = C/T, so it depends on temperature.
calculation: The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct, so we test each statement and look for the false one.
Statement A (diamagnetic susceptibility is independent of temperature): true. Diamagnetism arises in all atoms and hardly changes with temperature. So A is not the answer.
Statement B (ferromagnetic susceptibility depends on temperature): true. Above the Curie point it follows chi = C/(T - Tc). So B is not the answer.
Statement D (paramagnetic susceptibility depends on temperature): true. Curie's law says chi = C/T. So D is not the answer.
Statement C (paramagnetic susceptibility is independent of temperature): false, because Curie's law makes it depend on temperature.
So the incorrect statement is the one in option C.
questions.info: Above the Curie temperature a ferromagnet turns paramagnetic. Diamagnetic susceptibility is small and negative.
questions.trick: Paramagnetic = 1/T, ferromagnetic = 1/(T - Tc), diamagnetic = no T dependence.

questions.q: The area enclosed by a complete hysteresis loop on B-H curve of a ferromagnetic material denotes ______.
options: the energy dissipated in taking the specimen material during each complete cycle of magnetisation
questions.given: B-H hysteresis loop of a ferromagnet; meaning of the enclosed area.
questions.concept: Area of the B-H loop equals energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation.
calculation: Work done per unit volume in changing magnetisation by dH is H dB.
Over a full cycle, the total is the integral of H dB, which is the area of the loop.
This work is not recovered; it appears as heat in the material.
Coercivity and retentivity are intercepts of the loop on the H and B axes, not areas (options B, C, D).
So the loop area is the energy dissipated per cycle, which is option A.
questions.info: Soft iron has a narrow loop (low loss), so it is used in transformer cores. Steel has a wide loop, so it suits permanent magnets.
questions.trick: Area means energy loss; intercepts mean coercivity (on the H axis) and retentivity (on the B axis).
questions.formula: energy loss per cycle per volume = area of B-H loop

questions.q: The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit. This statement pertains to:
questions.given: Statement: induced emf equals rate of change of magnetic flux.
questions.concept: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: emf = -d(phi)/dt.
calculation: Read the statement: induced emf magnitude equals rate of change of magnetic flux.
This is exactly Faraday's law: emf = -d(phi)/dt.
Ampere's law relates magnetic field around a loop to the current through it (option B).
Gauss law relates electric flux to enclosed charge (option C).
Ohm's law relates voltage and current in a conductor (option D).
So the answer is option A.
questions.info: The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced emf opposes the change in flux. For N turns, emf = -N*d(phi)/dt.
questions.trick: Flux changing with time giving emf: always Faraday (with Lenz for direction).

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor (circular plates, R=6.0cm, C=100pF) is on a 230V AC supply at 320 rad/s. What is the RMS conduction current?
questions.given: R=6.0cm plates, C=100pF, V_rms=230V, omega=320 rad/s.
questions.concept: Capacitor in AC circuit: I_rms = V_rms / Xc, where Xc = 1/(omega*C), equivalently I_rms = V_rms*omega*C.
calculation: Formula: I_rms = V_rms / Xc, where Xc = 1/(omega*C). So I_rms = V_rms * omega * C.
Given: V_rms = 230 V, omega = 320 rad/s, C = 100 pF = 100 x 10^-12 F = 10^-10 F.
Plate radius R is not needed here.
7.36x10^-6 A = 7.36 microA, which matches option B.
questions.info: The plate radius R=6.0cm is a distractor here - it's only needed if you had to calculate C from geometry (C=epsilon0*A/d); since C is already given, it's irrelevant.
questions.trick: For a pure capacitor skip computing Xc separately - directly use I_rms=V_rms*omega*C, saving one division step.

questions.q: Series LCR circuit (R=30, XL=40, XC=80 ohms), 200V/50Hz AC source. Find the power dissipated.
questions.given: R=30 ohm, XL=40 ohm, XC=80 ohm, V_rms=200V.
questions.concept: Series LCR: Z=sqrt(R^2+(XL-XC)^2), I_rms=V_rms/Z, Power P=I_rms^2*R.
calculation: Formulas: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2), I_rms = V_rms/Z, P = I_rms^2 * R.
XL - XC = 40 - 80 = -40 ohm. Sign does not matter after squaring: (-40)^2 = 1600.
questions.info: Power is dissipated only in R; the inductor and capacitor store and return energy, consuming zero net power over a full cycle.
questions.trick: Spot 30-40-50 as a scaled 3-4-5 triangle via (XL-XC)=40, so Z comes out instantly without a calculator.

questions.q: An LC circuit: L=5.0x10^-2 H, C=5.0x10^-6 F. At t=0 all energy is in the capacitor. What is the angular frequency of oscillation?
questions.given: L=5.0x10^-2 H, C=5.0x10^-6 F, capacitor fully charged at t=0.
questions.concept: LC oscillation angular frequency: omega = 1/sqrt(LC).
calculation: Formula: omega = 1/sqrt(L*C).
This matches option B (2.0x10^3).
questions.info: An LC circuit is the electrical analogue of SHM - charge oscillates on the capacitor just like displacement in a spring-mass system, with L acting like mass and 1/C like the spring constant.
questions.trick: Write LC as a power of 10 that's a perfect square (here 25x10^-8) so sqrt comes out clean without a calculator.

questions.q: An LC circuit oscillates at 1.0 kHz; L=50 mH. Find C. (pi^2~10)
questions.concept: LC oscillation frequency: f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)), rearranged to C = 1/(4*pi^2*f^2*L).
calculation: Formula: f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)).
Square both sides: f^2 = 1/(4*pi^2*L*C). So C = 1/(4*pi^2*f^2*L).
Multiply by L: 4x10^7 * 0.05 = 2x10^6.
questions.info: The approximation pi^2~10 is a standard shortcut given specifically for LC numericals to avoid calculator-level precision.
questions.trick: Memorise C=1/(4*pi^2*f^2*L) as the direct rearranged formula, so you skip finding omega first and inverting afterward.

questions.q: An AC voltage is applied to a pure capacitor. The current ______ the voltage by ______.
questions.given: AC voltage applied to a pure (ideal) capacitor.
questions.concept: For a pure capacitor, i = C*dv/dt where v=v0*sin(omega*t); this gives current leading voltage by pi/2.
calculation: Let applied voltage be v = v0*sin(omega*t).
Charge on capacitor: q = C*v, so current i = dq/dt = C*(dv/dt).
Differentiate: i = C * v0 * omega * cos(omega*t).
Use cos(x) = sin(x + pi/2): i = i0 * sin(omega*t + pi/2), where i0 = omega*C*v0.
Current has phase (omega*t + pi/2), voltage has phase (omega*t). Current is ahead by pi/2 (90 degrees).
Other options are wrong: lagging is for an inductor, and a pi shift (opposite phase) does not occur in a pure capacitor.
So in a pure capacitor, current leads voltage by pi/2.
questions.info: This is the exact opposite of a pure inductor, where current LAGS voltage by pi/2 - a classic point of confusion in exam MCQs.
questions.trick: Use the mnemonic 'CIVIL': in a Capacitor I leads V, in an inductor L, V leads I - instant recall without deriving.

questions.q: AC source (220V, 50Hz) on a series LCR (R=12, XL=32, XC=16 ohms). Find the power dissipated and power factor.
questions.given: R=12 ohm, XL=32 ohm, XC=16 ohm, V_rms=220V.
questions.concept: Series LCR: Z=sqrt(R^2+(XL-XC)^2), I_rms=V_rms/Z, P=I_rms^2*R, power factor cos(phi)=R/Z.
calculation: Formulas: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (XL - XC)^2), I_rms = V_rms/Z, P = I_rms^2 * R, power factor = R/Z.
Power factor = cos(phi) = R/Z = 12/20 = 0.6.
So power = 1.452 kW and power factor = 0.6.
questions.info: Power factor cos(phi)=R/Z also tells you how resistive (close to 1) or reactive (close to 0) the circuit is - useful to sanity-check the computed power.
questions.trick: Once Z is found, power and power factor are each one quick line - no need to compute the phase angle phi explicitly.

questions.q: A sinusoidal voltage is applied to a series circuit containing a resistor of 25 ohm, a capacitor of 0.90 microF and an inductor of 100 mH. The frequency of the source can be varied. The frequency of the source that will create a resonance condition in the circuit is:
questions.given: R = 25 ohm, C = 0.90 microF = 0.90*10^-6 F, L = 100 mH = 0.1 H; find resonant frequency.
questions.concept: Series LCR resonance when X_L = X_C, so f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)).
calculation: Formula: at resonance X_L = X_C, giving f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). R does not affect it.
This is about 531 Hz, which matches option D.
questions.info: At resonance the impedance is minimum (Z = R) and the current is maximum. The resistance only controls the sharpness (quality factor) of the resonance.

questions.q: In a piezoelectric generator, the quartz crystal oscillates at the natural frequency of the LC tank circuit to produce ultrasonic waves of 1 MHz, with a capacitor of 25 nF in the tank circuit. The inductance of the coil used is nearly:
questions.given: f = 1 MHz = 10^6 Hz, C = 25 nF = 25*10^-9 F; find L.
questions.concept: Natural frequency of an LC circuit: f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)).
calculation: Formula: f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)), so L = 1/(4*pi^2*f^2*C).
L is nearly 1 microH, which is option C.
questions.info: Quartz vibrates at resonance when the oscillator frequency matches its natural frequency; this gives very stable frequency, used in ultrasonic generators and clocks. Question text was garbled in the source and answer follows the key.
questions.trick: With pi^2 about 10: L = 1/(4*10*f^2*C), which quickly gives 1 microH here.

questions.q: The average power supplied to an inductor over one complete cycle is ______.
questions.given: Pure inductor in an AC circuit; find average power over a full cycle.
questions.concept: In a pure inductor, current lags voltage by 90 degrees, so average power is zero.
calculation: Formula: P_avg = V_rms * I_rms * cos(phi), where phi is the phase difference.
For a pure inductor, current lags voltage by phi = 90 degrees.
cos(90 degrees) = 0.
So P_avg = V_rms * I_rms * 0 = 0.
Energy is stored in the magnetic field in one quarter cycle and returned in the next.
Average power over a full cycle is zero. Matches option A.
questions.info: A pure capacitor also consumes zero average power. Only resistance dissipates power in an AC circuit; this is why such current is called wattless current.
questions.trick: Pure L or pure C in AC means average power = 0 (power factor zero).

questions.q: In case of step-up transformer, which option is correct?
questions.given: Step-up transformer: secondary voltage is greater than primary voltage.
questions.concept: Step-up: N_s greater than N_p, K = N_s/N_p greater than 1, V_s greater than V_p, and secondary winding has more turns (more resistance).
calculation: Formula: (V_s)/(V_p) = (N_s)/(N_p) = K (transformer ratio).
A step-up transformer raises voltage, so V_s greater than V_p; option A is wrong.
This needs K greater than 1, so option B (K less than 1) is wrong.
It also needs N_s greater than N_p, so option D is wrong.
The secondary has more turns of (thinner) wire, so its resistance R_s is greater than R_p.
Only option C is correct.
questions.info: A step-up transformer steps current down (I_s less than I_p), so the primary uses thick wire with few turns and the secondary thin wire with many turns. Power stays nearly the same.
questions.trick: Step-up: more turns, more voltage, less current, and the secondary coil is the higher-resistance one.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of electromagnetic waves?
options: EM waves follow the principle of superposition
The electric vector causes optical effects
EM wave propagation needs no material medium
questions.given: Four statements about EM wave characteristics; identify the false one.
questions.concept: EM waves are produced by accelerated (not merely moving) charges; they obey superposition and propagate without a medium.
calculation: We need the statement that is FALSE for EM waves. Test each option.
Option A: EM waves obey superposition (they interfere and diffract). True, so not the answer.
Option B: The electric vector causes optical effects (eye and photographic film respond to it). True, so not the answer.
Option D: EM waves need no material medium and travel through vacuum. True, so not the answer.
Option C: Moving charges produce EM waves. A charge moving at constant velocity gives a steady current and a steady magnetic field, with no radiation.
Only an accelerated charge (changing velocity) radiates EM waves. So option C is false and is the answer.
questions.info: A charge moving at constant velocity has a field pattern that just travels along with it without radiating; radiation specifically requires acceleration (a changing velocity).
questions.trick: Watch for options that swap a precise term ('accelerating charges') for a looser one ('moving charges') - this exact substitution is a recurring exam trap.

questions.q: _______ use radio waves to transmit voice in the ultrahigh frequency band.
questions.given: A device using radio waves in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band to transmit voice.
questions.concept: EM spectrum classification: different radio services (AM, FM, TV, cellular) use different standard frequency bands.
calculation: We need the device that sends voice using the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band, 300 MHz to 3000 MHz.
AM radio: about 530 kHz to 1710 kHz, medium frequency. Not UHF, so it fails.
FM radio: about 88 MHz to 108 MHz, VHF band. Not UHF, so it fails.
TV waves: broadcast uses VHF and UHF, but the standard textbook match for UHF voice is not TV. Weaker fit, so it fails.
Cellular phones: work at about 800 MHz to 2000 MHz, which lies in UHF, and carry voice. This matches.
So the answer is Cellular phones.
questions.info: The standard NCERT table lists typical bands: AM in MF (530kHz-1710kHz), FM/TV in VHF, and mobile/cellular and satellite links in UHF (300MHz-3GHz).
questions.trick: Memorise the band-to-service mapping (AM-MF, FM/TV-VHF, cellular/satellite-UHF) since 'which service uses which band' questions recur often.

questions.q: A radio tunes 6 MHz to 10 MHz. The corresponding wavelength band is:
questions.given: Radio tuning range f=6 MHz to f=10 MHz.
questions.concept: Wave speed relation: c = f*lambda, so lambda = c/f, with c=3x10^8 m/s.
calculation: Formula: c = f * lambda, so lambda = c/f. Take c = 3x10^8 m/s.
Convert: 6 MHz = 6x10^6 Hz and 10 MHz = 10x10^6 = 10^7 Hz.
Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency, so the lower frequency gives the longer wavelength.
So the band is 50 m (at 6 MHz) to 30 m (at 10 MHz), which matches option A.
questions.info: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related, so the low-frequency end of any tuning range always corresponds to the long-wavelength end - a handy consistency check.
questions.trick: Compute lambda=c/f only at the two extreme frequencies and just flip the order (higher f gives shorter lambda) - no extra algebra needed.

questions.q: Which statements are correct? (a) Infrared waves are produced by hot bodies. (b) Sun is an important source of ultraviolet light.
questions.given: Statement (a): infrared from hot bodies. Statement (b): Sun emits significant UV.
questions.concept: EM spectrum facts: infrared radiation is emitted by hot/warm bodies; the Sun is a major source of ultraviolet radiation.
calculation: Check each statement separately.
Statement (a): Infrared waves are produced by hot bodies. Hot bodies emit heat radiation, which is mainly infrared. True.
Statement (b): The Sun is an important source of ultraviolet light. The Sun emits a lot of UV, most of it absorbed by the ozone layer. True.
Both (a) and (b) are true.
So the correct option is 'Both (a) and (b)'.
questions.info: The Sun's UV output is exactly why the ozone layer, which absorbs most solar UV, is critical for protecting life on Earth - a frequently tested application.
questions.trick: For 'which statements are true' MCQs, judge each statement fully independently first, then match the combination - don't let one statement's phrasing bias the other.

questions.q: Which EM wave/ray has the MINIMUM wavelength, among Gamma rays, Infrared, Ultraviolet, Visible?
questions.given: Compare wavelengths of Gamma rays, Infrared, Ultraviolet, Visible light.
questions.concept: EM spectrum ordering by increasing wavelength: Gamma rays < X-rays < Ultraviolet < Visible < Infrared < Microwave < Radio.
calculation: Order of EM spectrum from shortest to longest wavelength: Gamma, X-ray, Ultraviolet, Visible, Infrared, Microwave, Radio.
Visible light is about 400 nm to 700 nm.
Infrared is longer than visible (about 700 nm to 1 mm), so it is not the minimum.
Ultraviolet is shorter than visible (about 10 nm to 400 nm), but still longer than gamma rays.
Gamma rays have the highest frequency, and since lambda = c/f, they have the smallest wavelength (less than about 10^-11 m).
So the minimum wavelength is for Gamma rays.
questions.info: The full EM spectrum order (short to long wavelength) is: Gamma, X-ray, UV, Visible, Infrared, Microwave, Radio - worth memorising as one continuous chain.
questions.trick: Just recall the standard EM spectrum chain instead of comparing pairs - a minimum-wavelength question always picks the leftmost item in that chain.

questions.q: Which statements are correct? (a) EM waves have different speeds in different mediums. (b) Sound has different speeds in different mediums.
questions.given: Statement (a): EM waves have different speeds in different media. Statement (b): Sound has different speeds in different media.
questions.concept: Wave speed depends on the medium: EM wave speed in a medium = c/n (n = refractive index); sound speed depends on the medium's bulk modulus and density.
calculation: Check each statement separately.

Statement (a): Speed of EM waves in a medium is v = c/n, where n is the refractive index. n is different for glass, water and air, so the speed is different. Example: light is slower in glass than in vacuum. True.
Statement (b): Speed of sound depends on the medium. It is about 340 m/s in air, about 1500 m/s in water and about 5000 m/s in steel. True.
Both (a) and (b) are true.
So the correct option is 'Both (a) and (b)'.
questions.info: Unlike sound, EM waves can also travel through vacuum (at their fastest speed, c), while sound cannot travel through vacuum at all - a key conceptual difference.
questions.trick: When a question pairs an EM-wave claim with an analogous sound-wave claim, check each against its own physical dependency (refractive index vs bulk modulus/density) rather than assuming identical behaviour.

questions.q: Rank the wavelengths of Microwaves (l1), Gamma rays (l2), Ultraviolet (l3), Infrared (l4).
questions.given: Rank wavelengths of Microwaves (l1), Gamma rays (l2), Ultraviolet (l3), Infrared (l4).
questions.concept: EM spectrum order by decreasing wavelength: Radio/Microwave > Infrared > Visible > Ultraviolet > X-ray > Gamma rays.
calculation: Use the EM spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma.
Pick out the four given: Microwaves (l1), Infrared (l4), Ultraviolet (l3), Gamma rays (l2).
Microwave is first in this order, so l1 is the longest.
Infrared comes next, so l4 is less than l1 but greater than l3.
Ultraviolet comes after infrared, so l3 is greater than l2.
Gamma rays are last, so l2 is the shortest.
Order: l1 is greater than l4, which is greater than l3, which is greater than l2. This matches option C.
questions.info: This question tests the same EM spectrum sequence as the minimum-wavelength question above, just phrased as a four-way ranking - recognising the shared pattern saves re-deriving it.
questions.trick: Place all four waves onto the single memorised EM spectrum line (long to short: Radio/Microwave-Infrared-Visible-UV-Xray-Gamma) and read the order off directly.

questions.q: The amplitude of the electric field in a plane electromagnetic wave is 120 V/m. The amplitude of the magnetic field of the wave is:
questions.concept: In an EM wave E_0/B_0 = c, so B_0 = E_0/c.
calculation: Formula: E_0/B_0 = c, so B_0 = E_0/c.
This matches option D.
questions.info: E and B in an EM wave are in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation. Options B and C are huge numbers and cannot be a magnetic field amplitude.
questions.trick: In vacuum, B in tesla is E in V/m divided by 3*10^8, so multiply E by 3.3*10^-9: 120 x 3.3*10^-9 is about 4*10^-7.

questions.q: The characteristic impedance, as the ratio of the amplitudes of E- and H- vectors, in a plane electromagnetic wave in free space is nearly:
questions.given: Plane EM wave in free space; find Z0 = E0/H0.
questions.concept: Impedance of free space Z0 = E0/H0 = sqrt(mu0/eps0) = mu0*c.
calculation: Formula: Z0 = E0/H0 = sqrt(mu0/eps0) = mu0*c.
mu0 = 4*pi x 10^-7 H/m and c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
Z0 is nearly 376.7 ohm.
This is option B.
questions.info: Z0 is about 120*pi ohm, roughly 377 ohm. Its units are ohm since E is in V/m and H in A/m.
questions.trick: Remember Z0 = 120*pi = 377 ohm; options with 3.77 or 37.7 are just shifted decimals.

questions.q: In order to study internal atomic structure of crystals, we make use of electromagnetic radiations as ______.
questions.given: Choose the radiation suited to probing atomic structure of crystals.
questions.concept: Diffraction needs wavelength comparable to the spacing between atoms, about 1 angstrom; X-rays have this.
calculation: For diffraction by a crystal, wavelength must be about the same as the atomic spacing d, roughly 10^-10 m.
Visible light (400 to 700 nm) and ultraviolet (10 to 400 nm) are far longer than this.
So they cannot resolve atomic planes (option A, B and C fail).
X-rays have wavelengths from about 0.01 nm to 10 nm, close to the lattice spacing.
Bragg's law 2d*sin(theta) = n*lambda then gives the structure.
So the answer is option D.
questions.info: Max von Laue (1912) showed that crystals diffract X-rays, and the Braggs used this to find crystal structures like NaCl.
questions.trick: Atomic spacing about 1 angstrom, so choose X-rays (wavelength about 1 angstrom) for crystal structure questions.

questions.q: A 4.5cm candle is 30cm in front of a concave mirror (radius of curvature 42cm). At what screen distance is a sharp image formed?
questions.given: ho=4.5cm, u=-30cm, R=42cm (concave mirror).
questions.concept: Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, with f=-R/2 for a concave mirror (New Cartesian Convention).
calculation: Formulas: mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, and for a concave mirror f = -R/2 (New Cartesian sign convention).
Given: R = 42 cm, so f = -42/2 = -21 cm. Object distance u = -30 cm. The object height 4.5 cm is not needed for v.
v = -70 cm. Negative means the image is real and in front of the mirror.
So the screen must be placed 70 cm from the mirror.
questions.info: The negative sign on v tells you the image is real (same side as the object) - for a concave mirror with the object beyond the centre of curvature, the image always forms between F and C, real and inverted.
questions.trick: For mirror numericals, always convert R to f (f=R/2) first and keep the sign convention straight - most marks are lost to sign slips, not the algebra.

questions.q: An object is 10cm or 5cm from a concave mirror (radius of curvature 15cm). In which case is the image magnified, virtual, and erect?
questions.given: Concave mirror, R=15cm so f=-7.5cm. Case (a) u=-10cm, Case (b) u=-5cm.
questions.concept: Mirror formula 1/v+1/u=1/f and magnification m=-v/u; image is virtual when v comes out positive (behind the mirror).
calculation: Formulas: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, and m = -v/u. Concave mirror: f = -R/2 = -15/2 = -7.5 cm.
A virtual, erect image has positive v (behind the mirror) and positive m. Magnified means m greater than 1.
v = -30 cm. Negative v means a real image in front of the mirror.
m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-10) = -3. Negative m means inverted. So case (a) is real and inverted, not what we need.
v = +15 cm. Positive v means a virtual image behind the mirror.
m = -v/u = -15/(-5) = +3. Positive and greater than 1 means erect and magnified.
In case (b) the object (5 cm) is inside the focal length (7.5 cm), which gives a virtual, erect, magnified image. So the answer is Case (b), 5cm.
questions.info: This is the everyday shaving/makeup mirror situation - placing your face within the focal length (f=7.5cm here) of a concave mirror always gives a magnified, erect, virtual image.
questions.trick: No need to fully solve both cases - just check whether |u| is less than |f|; if the object is inside the focal length of a concave mirror, the image is automatically virtual, erect and magnified, so pick that case directly.

questions.q: A convex lens (f=50cm) is in contact with a concave lens (f=-40cm). Find the combined focal length and whether the system converges or diverges.
questions.given: Convex lens f1=+50cm in contact with concave lens f2=-40cm.
questions.concept: For thin lenses in contact, combined power adds: 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
calculation: Thin lenses in contact: powers add, so 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2. Use sign convention: convex f is positive, concave f is negative.
Take reciprocal: f = -200 cm.
Negative focal length means the combination is a diverging lens (the concave lens is stronger, as 40 is less than 50).
Combined focal length = 200 cm, diverging.
questions.info: Combining a weaker convex lens with a stronger concave lens always gives a net diverging system - the sign of the combined f is decided by whichever lens has the smaller magnitude of focal length (here the concave lens's 40cm beats the convex lens's 50cm).
questions.trick: Add powers in dioptres directly (P=1/f in metres): P = 1/0.5 - 1/0.4 = 2 - 2.5 = -0.5 D, so f = 1/P = -2m = -200cm - faster than juggling fractions in cm.

questions.q: Mirror A (concave) and mirror B (convex) are both made from the same 20cm-radius glass ball. Following New Cartesian convention, the focal lengths of A and B respectively are:
questions.given: Glass ball radius R=20cm, used to form concave mirror A and convex mirror B.
questions.concept: For a spherical mirror, f=-R/2 for a concave mirror and f=+R/2 for a convex mirror (New Cartesian Convention).
calculation: Both mirrors are cut from the same ball, so radius of curvature R = 20 cm for both.
Focal length of a spherical mirror: f = R/2 in magnitude, so |f| = 20/2 = 10 cm.
New Cartesian sign rule: concave mirror has focus in front of it (against incident light), so f is negative.
Concave mirror A: f = -10 cm.
Convex mirror has its focus behind it (along incident light), so f is positive.
Convex mirror B: f = +10 cm.
So A and B have f = -10 cm and +10 cm respectively.
questions.info: This is the classic 'silvered glass ball' question - the magnitude of f is the same (R/2) for both faces, only the sign flips between concave and convex under the New Cartesian Convention.
questions.trick: Don't recompute R separately for each mirror - since both come from one ball, R is identical, so you only need the sign rule (concave negative, convex positive) to answer in one line.

questions.q: A 3.0cm object is 9.0cm in front of a convex mirror (f=18.0cm). Find image distance and height (New Cartesian convention).
questions.given: ho=3.0cm, u=-9.0cm, convex mirror f=+18.0cm.
questions.concept: Mirror formula 1/v+1/u=1/f and magnification m=-v/u=hi/ho.
calculation: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification: m = -v/u = hi/ho.
Signs: object is in front, so u = -9.0 cm. Convex mirror, so f = +18.0 cm. ho = 3.0 cm.
v = +6 cm. Positive means image is behind the mirror (virtual, as always for a convex mirror).
So v = 6 cm and hi = 2.0 cm.
questions.info: A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for any real object position - that's why it's used as a vehicle side mirror, giving a wider field of view with a smaller image.
questions.trick: For convex mirrors you can skip worrying about sign ambiguity in the final answer - v always comes out positive and m always comes out positive (erect, smaller), so just match the magnitude to an option.

questions.q: A glass prism (n=3/2, refracting angle 60 deg) is immersed in water (n=4/3). Find the angle of minimum deviation.
questions.given: Prism angle A=60deg, glass n=3/2, surrounding medium is water n=4/3.
questions.concept: Minimum deviation formula: n_relative = sin((A+Dm)/2) / sin(A/2), where n_relative is the glass's refractive index relative to the surrounding medium.
calculation: For a prism at minimum deviation: n_relative = sin((A + Dm)/2) / sin(A/2). Here n_relative = n_glass / n_water.
A = 60 deg, so A/2 = 30 deg and sin(30 deg) = 1/2.
So (A + Dm)/2 = arcsin(9/16). Multiply both sides by 2: A + Dm = 2*arcsin(9/16).
Dm = 2*arcsin(9/16) - A. Convert A = 60 deg = pi/3 radians.
Dm = 2*arcsin(9/16) - pi/3.
questions.info: Whenever a prism is immersed in a medium denser than air, always use the RELATIVE refractive index (n_glass/n_medium) in the prism formula instead of the glass's index relative to air - this is the classic trap in this question type.
questions.trick: Recognise that immersing the prism in water just replaces the usual n with n_glass/n_medium in the same minimum-deviation formula - no new formula to memorise, just recompute the ratio first.

questions.q: An object is placed at a distance greater than twice the focal point distance from a concave mirror. The image formed by the mirror is:
options: real, inverted and magnification greater than one.
real, inverted and magnification less than one.
virtual, upright and magnification greater than one.
virtual, upright and magnification less than one.
questions.given: Object distance greater than 2f from a concave mirror (beyond the centre of curvature).
questions.concept: Concave mirror: object beyond C gives a real, inverted, diminished image between F and C.
calculation: Take a concave mirror with f = -10 cm (sign convention) and object at u = -30 cm, which is more than 2f.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, so 1/v = -1/10 + 1/30.
Negative v means the image is on the object side, so it is real.
Magnification m = -v/u = -(-15)/(-30) = -0.5.
Negative m means inverted, and |m| = 0.5 which is less than one, so diminished.
Real, inverted and diminished matches option B.
questions.info: A concave mirror gives a virtual, upright, magnified image only when the object is between the pole and the focus. Real images by a mirror are always inverted.
questions.trick: Object far away (beyond 2f) means a small real inverted image; moving the object closer makes the image bigger.

questions.q: A converging lens with two curved surfaces has a front surface with radius of curvature 10 cm and the back surface with radius of curvature 20 cm. It is made of material with refractive index 1.5. The focal length of the lens is:
questions.given: Biconvex lens: R_1 = +10 cm, R_2 = -20 cm, n = 1.5 (in air).
questions.concept: Lensmaker's formula: 1/f = (n - 1)*(1/R_1 - 1/R_2).
calculation: For a converging (biconvex) lens, R_1 = +10 cm and R_2 = -20 cm.
Positive f for a converging lens matches option A.
questions.info: For a biconvex lens the magnitudes of the radii simply add in reciprocal: 1/R_1 + 1/R_2. A converging lens always has positive focal length.
questions.trick: A converging lens must have positive f, so options B and D are out. Then (n-1)*(sum of curvatures) = 0.5 x 0.15 = 0.075 gives 13.3.

questions.q: The refractive index for a glass is 1.62. The sine of the critical angle for total internal reflection at a glass-air interface is:
questions.given: Refractive index of glass n = 1.62, glass to air interface.
questions.concept: Critical angle: sin(C) = 1/n for a ray going from a denser medium to air.
calculation: Formula: sin(C) = n_air/n_glass = 1/n.
Substitute n = 1.62.
1/1.62 = 0.617, which is about 0.62.
This matches option B.
questions.info: Total internal reflection needs the ray to go from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence to exceed the critical angle. Here C is about 38 degrees.
questions.trick: The sine of the critical angle is just the reciprocal of n, so no trig tables are needed: 1/1.62 is a little above 0.6.

questions.q: Which of the following has highest refractive index?
questions.given: Compare refractive indices of diamond, crown glass, water, dense flint glass.
questions.concept: Refractive index n = c/v; diamond has one of the highest values among common materials.
calculation: Recall approximate refractive indices of the listed materials.
Water: about 1.33 (option C).
Crown glass: about 1.52 (option B).
Dense flint glass: about 1.65 (option D).
Diamond: about 2.42 (option A).
Diamond has the highest refractive index. Matches option A.
questions.info: Diamond's high refractive index gives a small critical angle (about 24.4 degrees), so light undergoes total internal reflection repeatedly, making it sparkle.
questions.trick: Order to remember: water (1.33) less than crown glass (1.5) less than flint glass (1.6) less than diamond (2.4).

questions.q: Two identical coherent waves (intensity I each) undergo constructive interference. The resultant intensity is:
questions.given: Two coherent waves, each of intensity I, interfering constructively (phase difference=0).
questions.concept: Resultant intensity for two coherent sources: I_R = I1 + I2 + 2*sqrt(I1*I2)*cos(phi).
calculation: Formula: I_R = I1 + I2 + 2*sqrt(I1*I2)*cos(phi), where phi is the phase difference.
Constructive interference means phi = 0, so cos(phi) = 1.
Here I1 = I2 = I. Substitute: I_R = I + I + 2*sqrt(I*I)*1.
sqrt(I*I) = I, so the last term is 2*I.
Check: amplitudes add (a + a = 2a) and intensity goes as amplitude squared, so (2a)^2 = 4a^2, which is 4I.
questions.info: Constructive interference intensity (4I for equal amplitudes) is NOT simply I1+I2 (which would be 2I) - this difference between coherent and incoherent superposition is a very common MCQ trap.
questions.trick: Memorise the two extreme cases directly: constructive gives 4I (for equal intensities), destructive gives 0 - no need to redo the full formula each time when both sources have equal intensity.

questions.q: In Young's double slit experiment, slit separation d, wavelength lambda, screen distance D. The fringe width is given by:
questions.given: YDSE with slit separation d, wavelength lambda, screen distance D.
questions.concept: Fringe width in Young's double slit experiment: beta = lambda*D/d.
calculation: Let the screen be at distance D from slits S1 and S2 separated by d. Take a point P at height y from the centre.
Path difference at P = y*d/D (standard result for small angles, y much smaller than D).
Bright fringe needs path difference = n*lambda, so y*d/D = n*lambda.
This gives y_n = n*lambda*D/d.
Next bright fringe: y_(n+1) = (n+1)*lambda*D/d.
Fringe width = y_(n+1) - y_n = lambda*D/d * ((n+1) - n) = lambda*D/d.
So beta = lambda*D/d.
questions.info: Fringe width increases if D increases or decreases if d increases - this is why double slit setups use very closely spaced slits, to get wide, clearly visible fringes.
questions.trick: This is a pure formula-recall question - just remember beta=lambda*D/d (D in numerator since a farther screen spreads fringes out, d in denominator since wider slit separation compresses them).

questions.q: Sunlight scattering in the atmosphere (wavelength lambda): the amount of scattering is proportional to:
questions.given: Sunlight of wavelength lambda scattering in the atmosphere.
questions.concept: Rayleigh scattering law: scattering intensity is proportional to 1/lambda^4.
calculation: Rayleigh scattering law: scattered intensity is proportional to 1/lambda^4 (for particles much smaller than the wavelength, like air molecules).
Choice 1/lambda^4 matches Rayleigh law. Correct.
Choice lambda^4: this would mean longer wavelengths scatter more, but red light scatters less than blue. Wrong.
Options with power 2 (1/lambda^2, lambda^2): the law has power 4, not 2. Wrong.
Example: blue (about 400 nm) vs red (about 700 nm). Ratio = (700/400)^4 = (1.75)^4, about 9.4. So blue scatters about 9 times more.
That is why the sky looks blue and sunsets look red.
So scattering is proportional to 1/lambda^4.
questions.info: The same 1/lambda^4 law also explains why the sky looks blue rather than violet (even though violet scatters even more) - our eyes are more sensitive to blue and the sun emits more blue than violet light.
questions.trick: Just remember the inverse-fourth-power relation plus the sky/sunset examples - these questions are almost always direct recall of Rayleigh's law, not a calculation.

questions.q: A telescope (2.44m objective diameter), light wavelength 0.5 micron. Find its resolving power.
questions.given: Telescope objective diameter D=2.44m, light wavelength lambda=0.5 micron=0.5e-6 m.
questions.concept: Resolving power of a telescope (reciprocal of the limit of resolution): RP = 1/dtheta = D/(1.22*lambda).
calculation: Resolving power RP = 1/dtheta, where the limit of resolution dtheta = 1.22*lambda/D.
Convert units: lambda = 0.5 micron = 0.5 x 10^-6 m. D = 2.44 m.
questions.info: A bigger objective diameter D directly gives a finer resolving power (smaller dtheta) - this is the physical reason professional telescopes use huge mirrors/lenses, not just for light-gathering.
questions.trick: Plug numbers straight into RP = D/(1.22*lambda) without rearranging - the numbers here (2.44 and 1.22) are chosen to cancel neatly (2.44/1.22=2), keeping the arithmetic quick.

questions.q: In a Young's double slit experiment, waves of wavelength lambda are incident on the two slits in phase. They travel to a point on the screen to produce a second minimum of the interference pattern. The difference in the distance travelled by the waves is:
questions.given: Slits in phase; point is the second dark fringe (second minimum); find path difference.
questions.concept: Destructive interference: path difference = (2m - 1)*lambda/2, m = 1, 2, 3...
calculation: Formula: for minima, path difference = (2m - 1) x lambda/2, with m = 1 for the first minimum.
For the second minimum, m = 2.
path difference = (2 x 2 - 1) x lambda/2.
= 3 x lambda/2.
= 3*lambda/2, which matches option A.
questions.info: Minima occur at lambda/2, 3*lambda/2, 5*lambda/2 ... while maxima occur at 0, lambda, 2*lambda ... Do not confuse the second minimum with the path difference lambda.
questions.trick: First minimum is lambda/2, second is 3*lambda/2 (add lambda each time).

questions.q: Two ideal polaroid sheets are arranged so that the angle between the pass-axis of the two sheets is theta. An unpolarised beam of light of intensity I_0 is incident on one of the polaroids. If the intensity of light emerging from the other polaroid is I_0/4, the angle theta is:
questions.given: Unpolarised light I_0 passes through two ideal polaroids with relative angle theta; final intensity I_0/4.
questions.concept: Polaroid 1 halves unpolarised light; Malus's law: I = I_1*cos^2(theta) for polaroid 2.
calculation: Formula: after the first polaroid I_1 = I_0/2 (unpolarised light), then Malus's law I = I_1*cos^2(theta).
I = (I_0/2)*cos^2(theta).
Set this equal to I_0/4: (I_0/2)*cos^2(theta) = I_0/4.
Cancel I_0: cos^2(theta) = (1/4) x 2 = 1/2.
cos(theta) = 1/sqrt(2).
theta = 45 degrees, which matches option C.
questions.info: Unpolarised light always loses exactly half its intensity at the first polaroid, whatever its orientation. Malus's law applies only to already polarised light.
questions.trick: For two polaroids with unpolarised input, the fraction I/I_0 = (1/2)*cos^2(theta). Half of 1/2 is 1/4, so cos^2 is 1/2.

questions.q: In Young's double slit experiment, the slit separation is twice the wavelength of sodium light. The largest number of possible maxima on the screen is:
questions.given: Slit separation d = 2*lambda; find total number of bright fringes possible.
questions.concept: Maxima need d*sin(theta) = n*lambda, and sin(theta) cannot exceed 1.
calculation: Formula: condition for a bright fringe is d*sin(theta) = n*lambda, where n = 0, +-1, +-2, ...
Substitute d = 2*lambda: 2*lambda*sin(theta) = n*lambda.
Cancel lambda: sin(theta) = n/2.
sin(theta) can never be more than 1, so n/2 must be at most 1 in size. Hence n can be at most 2 in size.
Allowed values: n = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.
Count them: 5 maxima in total, which is option C.
questions.info: The central maximum (n = 0) is always one of the maxima. n = +-2 gives sin(theta) = 1, i.e. theta = 90 degrees, so those two fringes lie at the very edge (grazing) of the screen.
questions.trick: Maximum n = d/lambda. Total maxima = 2*(d/lambda) + 1 when d/lambda is a whole number: here 2*2 + 1 = 5.

questions.q: Interference fringes are obtained in Fresnel's biprism with sodium light of mean wavelength 589.3 nm. A thin transparent sheet of thickness 1.1 micrometre placed in the path of one beam shifts the central bright fringe by a distance equal to the fringe width. The refractive index of the sheet is nearly:
questions.given: lambda = 589.3 nm, t = 1.1 micrometre = 1100 nm, fringe shift = one fringe width.
questions.concept: Shift = (mu - 1)*t*D/d and fringe width = lambda*D/d.
calculation: Formula: shift of fringes = (mu - 1)*t*D/d; fringe width beta = lambda*D/d.
Shift = beta gives (mu - 1)*t*D/d = lambda*D/d.
D/d cancels: (mu - 1)*t = lambda.
mu is nearly 1.54, which is option D.
questions.info: A sheet adds an extra optical path of (mu - 1)*t. A shift of N fringes needs (mu - 1)*t = N*lambda. The fringes shift towards the side where the sheet is placed.
questions.trick: If the shift is one fringe, just do mu = 1 + lambda/t. Keep both in nm.
questions.formula: (mu - 1)*t = lambda (for a shift of one fringe)

questions.q: Brilliant colours observed on thin films of oily surface and soapy water arise due to the optical phenomenon of ______.
questions.given: Coloured patterns on oil films and soap bubbles.
questions.concept: Light reflected from top and bottom of a thin film interferes, giving colours.
calculation: Light falls on a thin film of oil or soap solution.
Part of it reflects from the top surface and part from the bottom surface.
The two reflected rays are coherent, since they come from the same source ray.
Their path difference depends on film thickness and wavelength, so some colours add up and others cancel.
This is interference, so the answer is option C.
questions.info: Dispersion in a prism needs a thick, shaped medium. In thin films the colours change with thickness and viewing angle, and a very thin film looks dark.
questions.trick: Colours on soap bubble or oil on road: think thin-film interference.

questions.q: Sunlight filtering through the space between the leaves of a tree often makes circular patches on the ground due to ______.
options: the phenomenon of refraction of light
the phenomenon of diffraction of light
the space between the leaves through which the sunlight penetrates
the phenomenon of scattering of light
questions.given: Circular bright patches under a tree in sunlight.
questions.concept: Light passing through small gaps bends and spreads (diffraction) as per the answer key.
calculation: Sunlight passes through small gaps between leaves.
Light bends around the edges of these small openings, which is diffraction.
Options A and D (refraction, scattering) do not explain shaped patches.
Option C only restates the gap and does not name a phenomenon.
The key answer is option B.
questions.info: Physically, round patches under trees are mostly pinhole images of the Sun (each gap acts like a pinhole camera). The answer key still marks diffraction, so follow that in this exam.
questions.trick: Among phenomena named in the options, pick diffraction for light through small gaps.

questions.q: Which one of the following optical phenomena gives evidence that light waves are transverse?
questions.given: Need the phenomenon that only transverse waves show.
questions.concept: Only transverse waves can be polarised, since vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
calculation: Interference and diffraction occur for all waves, longitudinal as well as transverse.
Rectilinear propagation is a general ray property and says nothing about wave type.
Polarization restricts vibrations to one plane perpendicular to propagation.
This is possible only if the vibrations are transverse.
So polarization gives the evidence, which is option B.
questions.info: Sound waves in air are longitudinal and cannot be polarised. Polarization of light was the key evidence that light is a transverse wave (Malus, Young, Fresnel).
questions.trick: 'Evidence for transverse nature' always means polarization.

questions.q: The phenomenon of polarization CANNOT occur in ______.
questions.given: Identify which wave cannot be polarized.
questions.concept: Polarization needs transverse vibrations; sound (acoustic) waves in air are longitudinal.
calculation: Polarization restricts vibrations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel.
So only transverse waves can be polarized.
Radio waves, X-rays and visible light are electromagnetic, hence transverse (options A, B, D can be polarized).
Acoustic waves in fluids are longitudinal, with vibration along the direction of travel.
So they cannot be polarized, which is option C.
questions.info: Polarization is the key proof that light is a transverse wave.
questions.trick: Longitudinal means no polarization. Sound in air is the standard example.

questions.q: In a Young's double slit experimental set-up, interference fringe pattern has been obtained with sodium light. If the entire experimental set-up were displaced from air and then immersed in clear water, contained in a suitable transparent tank, then the fringe pattern will likely ______.
questions.given: YDSE set-up moved from air into water (refractive index about 4/3).
questions.concept: Fringe width beta = lambda*D/d, and wavelength in a medium is lambda/n.
calculation: Formula: fringe width beta = lambda*D/d.
In water the wavelength becomes lambda' = lambda/n, with n = 4/3 for water.
D and d stay the same, since the whole set-up is immersed.
beta' = lambda'*D/d = (lambda/n)*D/d = beta/n.
beta' = (3/4)*beta, which is smaller than beta.
So the fringes shrink, which is option C.
questions.info: Frequency does not change when light enters a medium; speed and wavelength both reduce by the factor n.
questions.trick: Fringe width is proportional to wavelength, so a denser medium means narrower fringes.

questions.q: The working of Nicol prism is based on the optical phenomenon of ______.
questions.given: Principle behind a Nicol prism.
questions.concept: A Nicol prism splits unpolarized light by double refraction, then removes one ray by total internal reflection.
calculation: A Nicol prism is made from a calcite crystal cut and cemented with Canada balsam.
Unpolarized light entering calcite splits into an ordinary (o) ray and an extraordinary (e) ray; this is double refraction.
The o-ray meets the balsam layer at an angle larger than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected.
Only the e-ray comes out, plane polarized.
So the working is based on double refraction, which is option C.
questions.info: A Nicol prism acts as both a polarizer and an analyser.
questions.trick: Nicol prism or calcite means double refraction.

questions.q: In the Young's Double slit Experiment, two slits are made one millimeter apart and the screen is placed 1.5 m away. What is the fringe separation when blue-green light of wavelength 500 nm is used?
questions.concept: Fringe width in YDSE is beta = lambda*D/d.
calculation: Formula: fringe separation beta = lambda*D/d.
Convert units: lambda = 500 nm = 5*10^-7 m, d = 10^-3 m, D = 1.5 m.
Numerator = 7.5*10^-7.
7.5*10^-4 m = 0.75 mm. Matches option D.
questions.info: Fringe width grows with wavelength and screen distance, and shrinks with larger slit separation; dipping the set-up in water reduces it by the refractive index.
questions.trick: Convert to mm early: 500 nm = 5*10^-4 mm, so beta = 5*10^-4 * 1500 / 1 = 0.75 mm.

sections.heading: 13. Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter (5 questions)

questions.q: Light (energy flux 18 W/cm^2) falls on a non-reflecting surface (20 cm^2) at normal incidence. Find total momentum delivered (full absorption) over 30 minutes.
questions.given: Intensity = 18 W/cm^2, area = 20 cm^2, fully absorbing surface, duration = 30 minutes.
questions.concept: For light fully absorbed by a surface, momentum delivered = total energy absorbed / c (since photon momentum p = E/c); first find power = intensity*area, then energy = power*time.
calculation: Power falling on the surface: P = intensity * area = 18 W/cm^2 * 20 cm^2 = 360 W.
Energy absorbed: E = P*t = 360 * 1800 = 648000 J = 6.48x10^5 J.
Light has momentum p = E/c. Fully absorbed (non-reflecting) means all of this momentum is delivered once (no doubling).
p = 2.16x10^-3 kg*m/s. Unit check: E/c is J/(m/s) = kg*m/s.
questions.info: If the surface were perfectly reflecting instead of fully absorbing, the momentum delivered would double (p = 2*Energy/c), since the photon's momentum reverses direction rather than being absorbed.
questions.trick: Convert everything to base SI units first (W/cm^2 * cm^2 cancels directly to watts, minutes to seconds) before plugging into p=E/c, to avoid unit-juggling errors mid-calculation.

questions.q: A photocathode has a work function of 2.4 eV. It is illuminated with monochromatic radiation whose photon energy is 3.9 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons produced is:
questions.given: Work function = 2.4 eV, photon energy = 3.9 eV, 1 eV = 1.6*10^-19 J.
questions.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: K_max = h*f - work function.
calculation: Formula: K_max = (photon energy) - (work function).
Convert to joules: 1 eV = 1.6*10^-19 J.
This matches option A.
questions.info: The stopping potential here is 1.5 V, since K_max = e*V_0. Also, the kinetic energy is the maximum value; electrons from deeper in the metal come out with less.
questions.trick: Subtract in eV first, then convert once: 1.5 eV x 1.6*10^-19 = 2.4*10^-19 J. Option A is the only one in that range.

questions.q: A proton is moving at a speed of 5.0 x 10^4 m/s. The de Broglie wavelength associated with it is ______. (m_p = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s)
questions.concept: de Broglie wavelength: lambda = h/(m*v).
calculation: Formula: lambda = h/(m*v).
lambda = 0.794*10^-11 m, which is about 0.79*10^-11 m, matching option B.
questions.info: Lambda is inversely proportional to momentum, so a heavier or faster particle has a shorter wavelength. For the same speed an electron has a wavelength about 1836 times larger than a proton.
questions.trick: Estimate: 6.63/8.35 is a bit under 0.8, and the power is 10^-11. Only option B fits.

questions.q: Which one of the following particles in motion, having the same velocity, has the longest wavelength?
questions.given: All particles move with the same velocity v.
questions.concept: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/(m*v); for the same v, lambda is inversely proportional to mass.
calculation: Formula: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/(m*v).
h and v are the same for all four particles, so lambda is proportional to 1/m.
Longest wavelength means the smallest mass.
Masses: electron about 9.1*10^-31 kg, proton and neutron about 1.67*10^-27 kg, alpha about 6.6*10^-27 kg.
The electron is the lightest, so it has the longest wavelength, which is option C.
questions.info: Electron wavelength is why electron microscopes can resolve far finer detail than light microscopes.
questions.trick: Same velocity: lightest particle wins. Same energy or potential: formula changes, so read carefully.

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated in a field of same potential difference. Then, the ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths associated with the moving material particles is:
questions.given: Proton (m, q) and alpha particle (4m, 2q) accelerated through the same potential V; find lambda_p : lambda_alpha.
questions.concept: de Broglie wavelength of a charge accelerated through V: lambda = h/sqrt(2*m*q*V).
calculation: Formula: lambda = h/p = h/sqrt(2*m*q*V).
For the same V, lambda is proportional to 1/sqrt(m*q).
Proton: m*q = m x q = mq.
Alpha: m*q = 4m x 2q = 8mq.
lambda_p/lambda_alpha = sqrt(8mq/mq) = sqrt(8).
sqrt(8) = 2*sqrt(2).
So the ratio is 2*sqrt(2) : 1, which is option A.
questions.info: For an electron accelerated through V volts, lambda = 12.27/sqrt(V) angstrom.
questions.trick: Same V: lambda is proportional to 1/sqrt(mq). Take the product mq for each particle (alpha has 4 x 2 = 8 times a proton) and take its square root.

questions.q: An alpha particle (KE 20 MeV) heads toward a stationary tin nucleus (Z=50). Find the distance of closest approach.
questions.given: Alpha particle KE = 20 MeV, target = tin nucleus with Z=50.
questions.concept: At closest approach all KE converts to electrostatic PE: KE = (1/4*pi*eps0)*(2e)(Ze)/d, i.e. d = 2*k*Z*e^2/KE (k=9x10^9, alpha charge=2e).
calculation: At closest approach the alpha stops, so all its KE becomes electrostatic PE: KE = k*(2e)*(Ze)/d.
Solve for d: d = 2*Z*k*e^2 / KE. Here Z = 50, k = 9x10^9, e = 1.6x10^-19 C.
questions.info: At closest approach the alpha particle momentarily has zero velocity, so all its KE sits as electrostatic PE - this is exactly how Rutherford first estimated that the nucleus is far smaller than the atom.
questions.trick: Memorise d = (2*k*Z*e^2)/KE(in joules) as one formula, converting MeV to joules via 1 MeV = 1.6x10^-13 J, so you don't re-derive Coulomb energy balance each time.

questions.q: The energy equivalent of the rest mass of an electron is nearly:
questions.given: Electron rest mass m = 9.11x10^-31 kg, c = 3x10^8 m/s.
questions.concept: Einstein mass-energy equivalence: E = m*c^2, then convert joules to eV (1 eV = 1.6x10^-19 J).
calculation: Mass-energy relation: E = m*c^2. Here m = 9.11x10^-31 kg and c = 3x10^8 m/s.
Convert to eV by dividing by 1.6x10^-19: E = 8.2x10^-14 / 1.6x10^-19 = 5.12x10^5 eV.
1 MeV = 10^6 eV, so E = 0.512 MeV.
This is about 0.511 MeV (small difference is due to rounding of c).
Quick check of others: 51.1, 1.51 and 5.11 MeV are 10 times or more off. Wrong.
questions.info: This 0.511 MeV value is a standard constant used throughout particle physics - for example, each photon from electron-positron annihilation carries exactly 0.511 MeV.
questions.trick: Just memorise 0.511 MeV as the electron rest energy directly instead of recomputing m*c^2 every time it appears.

questions.q: A 4.50 MeV alpha particle approaches a uranium nucleus (Z=92) head-on. The distance of closest approach is close to:
questions.given: Alpha particle KE = 4.50 MeV, target = uranium nucleus with Z=92.
questions.concept: Same closest-approach relation: d = 2*k*Z*e^2/KE (k=9x10^9, alpha charge=2e).
calculation: Closest approach: KE = k*(2e)*(Ze)/d, so d = 2*Z*k*e^2 / KE. Here Z = 92.
Convert: 5.89x10^-14 m = 58.9x10^-15 m = 58.9 fm, close to 59 fm.
questions.info: Larger Z (uranium vs tin) and lower KE both push the closest-approach distance up, showing d scales directly with Z and inversely with KE.
questions.trick: Reuse the same k*e^2 = 2.304x10^-28 constant across every closest-approach question in this chapter - only Z and KE change.

questions.q: Packing fraction and binding energy both determine nuclear stability. Which statement is correct?
options: Higher packing fraction, lower binding energy
Same packing fraction and binding energy
Lower packing fraction, lower binding energy
Lower packing fraction, higher binding energy
questions.given: Comparing packing fraction and binding energy as nuclear-stability indicators.
questions.concept: Packing fraction f = (isotopic mass - mass number)/mass number; binding energy per nucleon = (mass defect)*c^2/A - these two trends run opposite to each other.
calculation: Packing fraction f = (isotopic mass - mass number) / mass number. Binding energy per nucleon shows how tightly bound the nucleus is.
A tightly bound nucleus has lost more mass as binding energy, so its isotopic mass is smaller. So f is lower (more negative).
So low packing fraction goes with high binding energy. The two trends are opposite.
Example: near iron-56, binding energy per nucleon is highest and packing fraction is lowest. This is the most stable region.
Choice (higher f, lower BE): this also fits the opposite trend, but it describes loosely bound, less stable nuclei. The standard stability answer is low f with high BE, so this is not the key.
Choice (same f and BE): they are not the same. Wrong.
Choice (lower f, lower BE): lower f means higher BE, not lower. Wrong.
Choice (lower f, higher BE) matches. Correct.
questions.info: The packing-fraction curve and the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve versus mass number A are essentially mirror images of each other, both showing a stability peak near A≈56 (iron).
questions.trick: Packing fraction and binding energy per nucleon always move in OPPOSITE directions - pick whichever option states the opposite trend.

questions.q: An electron in orbit n=2 (Bohr model, hydrogen). Find the magnetic dipole moment. (e/m=1.76x10^11 C/kg, h/2pi=1.05x10^-34 J.s)
questions.concept: Orbital magnetic moment mu = (e/2m)*L, where angular momentum L is quantised as L = n*(h/2pi) (Bohr model).
calculation: Orbital magnetic moment: mu = (e/2m) * L. Bohr rule: L = n*(h/2pi).
Rounded, mu = 1.85x10^-23 A*m^2.
questions.info: For n=1 this same formula gives the Bohr magneton (9.27x10^-24 A*m^2), the fundamental unit of orbital magnetic moment used throughout atomic and quantum physics.
questions.trick: Combine the two steps into one formula, mu = n*(e/2m)*(h/2pi), to avoid separately writing out L before plugging into mu.

questions.q: Rutherford scattering proved the:
questions.given: Rutherford's alpha-particle gold-foil scattering experiment.
questions.concept: Large-angle alpha scattering implies a small, dense, positively charged core inside an otherwise empty atom.
calculation: Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Look at what was seen and what it means.
Observation 1: most alpha particles went straight through. Meaning: atom is mostly empty space.
Observation 2: a few alpha particles deflected by large angles, some even came back (more than 90 degrees).
Such strong deflection needs a very small, dense, positively charged centre that repels alpha particles.
Choice (electron): found earlier by J.J. Thomson, not shown by this experiment. Wrong.
Choice (existence of atom): atoms were already accepted. Wrong.
Choice (mass of nucleus): the experiment did not measure its mass. Wrong.
So the experiment proved the presence of the nucleus. Correct.
questions.info: The same closest-approach calculation used elsewhere in this chapter (KE = PE at the point of nearest approach) is how Rutherford estimated the nuclear size as about 10^-14 m, vastly smaller than the atom's 10^-10 m size.
questions.trick: Whenever a question mentions large-angle/back-scattering of alpha particles, the answer is almost always 'presence of nucleus' - a recognizable keyword pattern.

questions.q: A radioactive decay constant is 0.00693 per year. What is the half-life? (ln2=0.693)
questions.given: Decay constant lambda = 0.00693 per year, ln2 = 0.693.
questions.concept: Half-life relation for radioactive decay: T(1/2) = ln2/lambda.
calculation: Half-life formula: T(1/2) = ln2 / lambda.
Given: ln2 = 0.693 and lambda = 0.00693 per year.
Write 0.00693 = 0.693 / 100, so the ratio is 100.
T(1/2) = 100 years. Unit is years because lambda is per year.
questions.info: Decay constant has units of inverse time, so the half-life comes out automatically in whatever time unit lambda was given in - here years.
questions.trick: ln2=0.693 is fixed, so whenever lambda is given as '0.00xyz', dividing 0.693 by it usually lands on a clean round number - a built-in sanity check on your arithmetic.

questions.q: Bohr model: find the photon energy for a transition from the 3rd excited state (n=4) to the ground state (n=1).
questions.given: Hydrogen atom, Bohr model, transition from n=4 to n=1.
questions.concept: Photon energy for a Bohr transition: delta-E = 13.6*(1/n_final^2 - 1/n_initial^2) eV.
calculation: Hydrogen energy levels: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV.
Initial level n = 4: E_4 = -13.6 / 16 = -0.85 eV.
Final level n = 1: E_1 = -13.6 / 1 = -13.6 eV.
Photon energy = E_initial - E_final = E_4 - E_1 = -0.85 - (-13.6).
Energy is positive, as expected for an emitted photon.
questions.info: This n=4 to n=1 transition belongs to the Lyman series (all transitions ending at n=1), which lies in the ultraviolet region, not in visible light.
questions.trick: Use the combined formula delta-E = 13.6*(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2) eV directly instead of computing E_4 and E_1 as two separate lines.

questions.q: Bohr model, hydrogen: electron transitions from n=2 to n=1. Find the emitted photon's frequency. (R=1.0x10^7 /m)
questions.given: Hydrogen atom, n=2 to n=1 transition, Rydberg constant R = 1.0x10^7 /m.
questions.concept: Rydberg formula: 1/lambda = R*(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2), then photon frequency f = c/lambda.
calculation: Rydberg formula: 1/lambda = R * (1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2). Here n_f = 1, n_i = 2, R = 1.0x10^7 per m.
Frequency f = c/lambda = c * (1/lambda). Take c = 3x10^8 m/s.
questions.info: This n=2 to n=1 line is the Lyman-alpha transition, the strongest UV emission line of hydrogen, widely used as a marker in astronomy.
questions.trick: Combine both steps into f = c*R*(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2) in one go rather than finding lambda first and then inverting it separately.

questions.q: Which spectral series lies in the VISIBLE region of the hydrogen spectrum?
questions.given: Hydrogen spectral series: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett.
questions.concept: Series are classified by the final energy level n_f they end on: n_f=1 Lyman (UV), n_f=2 Balmer (visible), n_f=3,4,5 Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (infrared).
calculation: Each hydrogen series is named by the level the electron lands on (n_f).
Lyman: n_f = 1. Big energy gaps, so ultraviolet. Not visible.
Balmer: n_f = 2. Photon energies about 1.9 to 3.4 eV, which is visible light (red to violet).
Paschen: n_f = 3. Smaller gaps, so infrared. Not visible.
Brackett: n_f = 4. Even smaller gaps, infrared. Not visible.
Memory trick: Lyman UV, Balmer visible, Paschen and others infrared.
So the visible series is the Balmer series.
questions.info: The Balmer series includes the famous H-alpha line (656 nm, red) and H-beta line (486 nm, blue-green), heavily used in astronomy to study stars and nebulae.
questions.trick: Memorise the single sequence 'Lyman=UV, Balmer=Visible, Paschen/Brackett/Pfund=IR' by final n-level - it answers nearly every 'which series lies in region X' question instantly.

questions.q: The wavelength of the line in the Balmer series of hydrogen spectrum corresponding to the transition from n=4 to n=2 level is: (R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1)
questions.given: Hydrogen, transition n = 4 to n = 2 (Balmer), R = 1.097*10^7 per m.
questions.concept: Rydberg formula: 1/lambda = R*(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2), with n_1 = 2 for the Balmer series.
calculation: Formula: 1/lambda = R x (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2), with n_1 = 2 and n_2 = 4.
lambda = 486 nm, which matches option C.
questions.info: This 486 nm line is H-beta (blue-green), the second Balmer line. H-alpha (n=3 to 2) is the red line at about 656 nm.
questions.trick: Memorise Balmer lines: 656 nm (n=3), 486 nm (n=4), 434 nm (n=5), 410 nm (n=6).

questions.q: According to Bohr model, the radius of the electron orbit in the n=1 level of the hydrogen atom is 0.053 nm. The radius for the n=3 level is:
questions.given: r_1 = 0.053 nm for n = 1 of hydrogen; find r for n = 3.
questions.concept: Bohr orbit radius scales as n^2: r_n = n^2*r_1.
calculation: Formula: r_n = n^2 x r_1 for hydrogen.
r_3 = 0.477 nm, which matches option D.
questions.info: The Bohr radius a_0 = 0.053 nm is the n=1 radius. For a hydrogen-like ion of charge Z the radius becomes n^2*a_0/Z, and orbital speed goes as Z/n.
questions.trick: Radius goes as n^2 (1, 4, 9 ...), so n=3 is 9 times larger, and only option D is about nine times 0.053.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is 5.5 h. If there are initially 48 x 10^32 atoms of this isotope, the number of atoms of the isotope remaining after 22 h is:
questions.given: T_half = 5.5 h, N_0 = 48 x 10^32, t = 22 h; find N.
questions.concept: Number remaining after n half-lives is N = N_0 / 2^n, where n = t / T_half.
calculation: Formula: N = N_0 / 2^n, where n = t / T_half.
n = 22 / 5.5 = 4 half-lives.
N = 3 x 10^32. Matches option A.
questions.info: Fraction left after n half-lives is (1/2)^n; after 4 half-lives only 1/16 (6.25 percent) remains.
questions.trick: Halve repeatedly: 48 to 24 to 12 to 6 to 3 (four halvings) - quicker than using exponents.

questions.q: A nucleus with atomic number Z and mass number A emits an alpha particle. The atomic number and mass number, respectively, of the daughter nucleus are:
questions.given: Parent nucleus (Z, A) emits an alpha particle (2 protons, 2 neutrons).
questions.concept: Alpha particle is He-4 nucleus: it carries away 2 units of charge and 4 units of mass number.
calculation: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: atomic number 2, mass number 4.
Conservation of charge: Z = Z' + 2, so Z' = Z - 2.
Conservation of mass number: A = A' + 4, so A' = A - 4.
Daughter nucleus has atomic number Z-2 and mass number A-4. Matches option C.
questions.info: Beta-minus decay gives (Z+1, A) and gamma emission changes neither Z nor A.
questions.trick: Alpha: Z down by 2, A down by 4. Beta: Z up by 1, A same.
questions.formula: Z to Z-2, A to A-4

questions.q: The speed of a fast moving electron, having energy of 3 MeV, in terms of speed of light in vacuum c, is:
questions.given: Electron with total energy E = 3 MeV; rest energy E0 = 0.511 MeV; find v/c.
questions.concept: Total energy E = gamma*E0 and gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
calculation: Formula: E = gamma*E0, where gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) and E0 = 0.511 MeV for an electron.
Here the quoted 3 MeV is the total energy, so gamma = E/E0 = 3/0.511.
gamma = 5.871.
So v = 0.985 c, which is option A.
questions.info: If 3 MeV were the kinetic energy instead, gamma would be 6.87 and v would be 0.989 c, which is not an option, so the question means total energy.
questions.trick: Electron rest energy is 0.511 MeV, so any energy of a few MeV means v is very close to c. Use v/c = sqrt(1 - (E0/E)^2) directly.

questions.q: Total energy of a moving particle is twice its rest mass energy. Then, the ratio of its relativistic speed to the speed of light in vacuum will be:
questions.given: Total energy E = 2*E0 (E0 = rest mass energy); find v/c.
questions.concept: E = gamma*E0, so gamma = 2; then v/c = sqrt(1 - 1/gamma^2).
calculation: Formula: E = gamma*E0 with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
E = 2*E0 gives gamma = 2.
v/c = sqrt(3)/2.
So the ratio v : c = sqrt(3) : 2, which is option D.
questions.info: Kinetic energy here equals E0 (K = E - E0 = E0). A particle with gamma = 2 moves at about 86.6 percent of c.
questions.trick: Memorise: gamma = 2 gives v/c = sqrt(3)/2 and gamma = 5/4 gives v/c = 3/5.

questions.q: Which option represents the law of radioactive decay?
questions.given: Choose the correct exponential decay law.
questions.concept: Number of undecayed nuclei decreases exponentially with time at rate lambda.
calculation: The decay rate is proportional to the number of nuclei: dN/dt = -lambda*N.
Separate variables: dN/N = -lambda*dt.
Integrate: ln N = -lambda*t + constant.
Using N = N(0) at t = 0: N(t) = N(0) * e^(-lambda*t).
Option A and B have positive exponents (growth), and option C has wrong form with t in the denominator.
Matches option D.
questions.info: Half-life T_half = 0.693/lambda and mean life tau = 1/lambda; after one mean life N falls to N(0)/e (about 37 percent).
questions.trick: Decay means a negative exponent with lambda*t only, no extra factors.

questions.q: A circuit of two NOR gates - identify the truth table and logic operation performed.
questions.given: A logic circuit built from two NOR gates in cascade.
questions.concept: NOR output = NOT(A OR B); feeding a NOR gate's output into a second NOR gate as its own inverter recovers OR: NOT(NOT(A OR B)) = A OR B.
calculation: NOR gate: output = NOT(A OR B). It gives 1 only when both inputs are 0.
Circuit: first NOR takes A and B and gives Y1 = NOT(A OR B).
Second NOR has both inputs joined to Y1, so Y2 = NOT(Y1 OR Y1) = NOT(Y1). It works as a NOT gate.
Y2 = NOT(NOT(A OR B)) = A OR B (double negation cancels).
Truth table, (A,B) gives Y2: (0,0) gives Y1 = 1, so Y2 = 0.
(0,1) gives Y1 = 0, so Y2 = 1.
(1,0) gives Y1 = 0, so Y2 = 1. (1,1) gives Y1 = 0, so Y2 = 1.
Output is 0,1,1,1 which is the OR gate. AND would be 0,0,0,1 and NAND 1,1,1,0, so those fail.
questions.info: NOR and NAND are both called universal gates because any logic gate (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, etc.) can be built using only NOR gates or only NAND gates.
questions.trick: Memorise the two standard combos directly: NOR + NOR(as inverter) = OR, and NAND + NAND(as inverter) = AND - most 'identify the gate from two gates' questions reduce to one of these.
questions.formula: NOT(NOT(A OR B)) = A OR B

questions.q: A pure Si crystal (6x10^28 atoms/m^3) is doped with 1 ppm pentavalent As. (ni=1.5x10^16 m^-3). Find the electron and hole concentrations.
questions.given: Pure Si: 6x10^28 atoms/m^3, doped with 1 ppm pentavalent As, ni = 1.5x10^16 m^-3.
questions.concept: n-type doping: donor concentration ND sets majority electron concentration n_e ≈ ND; law of mass action n_e*n_h = ni^2 gives minority hole concentration.
calculation: Given: Si atoms = 6x10^28 per m^3. Doping = 1 ppm = 1 part in 10^6 = 10^-6. ni = 1.5x10^16 per m^3.
Arsenic is pentavalent, so each As atom gives one free electron (n-type). Donor density N_D = 6x10^28 * 10^-6 = 6x10^22 per m^3.
Majority electrons: n_e is about N_D = 6x10^22 per m^3 (ni is much smaller than N_D, so ni contribution is negligible).
Mass action law: n_e * n_h = ni^2. So n_h = ni^2 / n_e.
So n_e = 6x10^22 and n_h = 3.75x10^9 per m^3.
questions.info: Even though hole concentration crashes from the intrinsic 1.5x10^16 down to 3.75x10^9, the product n_e*n_h stays exactly equal to ni^2 regardless of doping level - a useful invariant to check your work.
questions.trick: For n-type doping, just set majority (electron) concentration equal to the donor doping concentration directly, then get the minority (hole) concentration via ni^2/n_e - skips unnecessary algebra.

questions.q: A Zener diode is a ______ doped PN junction diode, connected in ______ bias.
questions.given: Zener diode PN junction - doping level and bias direction.
questions.concept: Zener diodes use heavy doping on both sides to create a very thin depletion layer, enabling field-induced (Zener) breakdown at a well-defined reverse voltage.
calculation: A Zener diode is made for breakdown at a sharp, fixed reverse voltage.
Doping: heavy doping on both sides makes the depletion layer very thin.
A thin layer gives a very strong electric field even at a small reverse voltage, which pulls electrons out of bonds (Zener breakdown).
Light doping would give a wide depletion layer and a high, unsteady breakdown. So 'lightly' is wrong.
Bias: in forward bias it acts like an ordinary diode and does not regulate voltage. So 'forward' is wrong.
In reverse bias the voltage across it stays nearly constant after breakdown, so it is used as a voltage regulator.
So it is heavily doped and used in reverse bias.
questions.info: Zener breakdown (heavy doping, thin depletion layer, field-induced) occurs at low voltages, while avalanche breakdown (lighter doping, thicker depletion layer, collision-induced) occurs at higher voltages - both are reverse-bias phenomena but via different mechanisms.
questions.trick: Lock 'Zener = heavily doped + reverse bias' together as one phrase - any option mentioning 'lightly doped' or 'forward bias' can be eliminated immediately.

questions.q: An acceptor replacement atom in silicon might have n electrons in its outer shell. The value of n is:
questions.given: Silicon has 4 valence electrons; acceptor impurity replaces a Si atom.
questions.concept: Acceptor (trivalent, group 13) impurity has 3 valence electrons and creates holes, making p-type material.
calculation: Silicon is in group 14 and has 4 electrons in its outer shell.
An acceptor impurity must have fewer valence electrons than Si so that a hole is created.
Acceptors are trivalent atoms such as B, Al, Ga, In.
Such an atom has 3 electrons in its outer shell, so n = 3. Matches option D.
questions.info: Donors are pentavalent (P, As, Sb) giving n-type; acceptors are trivalent giving p-type, and both keep the crystal electrically neutral.
questions.trick: Acceptor means 3 valence electrons (p-type); donor means 5 (n-type).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of trivalent impurity in intrinsic semiconductors?
questions.given: Options: In, As, Al, B.
questions.concept: Trivalent (group 13) dopants make p-type; arsenic is group 15 (pentavalent).
calculation: Trivalent impurities have 3 valence electrons (group 13) and create holes (p-type).
Indium (In) is group 13, so trivalent.
Aluminium (Al) is group 13, so trivalent.
Boron (B) is group 13, so trivalent.
Arsenic (As) is group 15 with 5 valence electrons, so pentavalent (n-type donor).
So As is NOT trivalent. Matches option B.
questions.info: Trivalent dopants are called acceptors; pentavalent dopants (P, As, Sb) are called donors.
questions.trick: Remember BAGI for trivalent (B, Al, Ga, In); P, As, Sb are the pentavalent ones.
questions.formula: Trivalent: B, Al, Ga, In; Pentavalent: P, As, Sb

questions.q: In a Zener-regulated power supply a Zener diode with V_Z = 5.0 V is used for regulation. The load current is to be 5.0 mA and the unregulated input is 10.0 V. What should be the value of series resistor R_S? Let Zener current I_Z = 20 mA.
questions.given: V_Z = 5 V, V_in = 10 V, I_L = 5 mA, I_Z = 20 mA.
questions.concept: Series resistor carries Zener plus load current; it drops the excess input voltage.
calculation: Formula: R_S = (V_in - V_Z)/(I_Z + I_L), because the current through R_S splits into Zener and load.
Voltage drop across R_S = 10 - 5 = 5 V.
Total current through R_S = I_Z + I_L = 20 mA + 5 mA = 25 mA = 0.025 A.
This matches option C.
questions.info: A Zener diode works in reverse breakdown; if load current drops, the extra current just flows through the Zener, holding V_Z steady.
questions.trick: Divide in mA: 5 V / 25 mA = 0.2 kilo-ohm = 200 ohm.

questions.q: The truth table shown below corresponds to which logic gate? [Table: A,B then Y: 0,0 gives 1; 0,1 gives 1; 1,0 gives 1; 1,1 gives 0]
questions.given: Outputs: 00 gives 1, 01 gives 1, 10 gives 1, 11 gives 0.
questions.concept: Output is 0 only when both inputs are 1: that is NAND (AND followed by NOT).
calculation: List the outputs: Y = 1 for (0,0), (0,1), (1,0) and Y = 0 only for (1,1).
An AND gate gives 1 only for (1,1); the given table is exactly its complement.
So Y = NOT(A AND B), which is a NAND gate.
NOR would give 1 only for (0,0); OR would give 0 only for (0,0); NOT has a single input.
Matches option A.
questions.info: NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any other gate can be built using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.
questions.trick: Check the odd row: a single 0 at (1,1) means NAND; a single 1 at (0,0) means NOR.
